Charles H. Alexander is a native Californian, having been born and
raised in Chico. He and his wife, Greta, had been married for forty-four years at
the time of his Installation as Grand Master. They have two sons, and are the
pro ud grandparents of three grandchildren. His is a member of a five-generation
Califo rnia Masonic family. His great-grandfather, Allen Alexander, signed the
Charter of Snow Mountain Lodge No. 271; his grandfather. his father, and both
his sons became members of the Craft. Our Grand Master was Initiated an
Entered Apprentice Mason on January 25, 1949; Passed to the Degree of Fellow
Craft on March I 8, I 949; and Raised a Master Mason on May 3, 1949, in Chico
Lodge No. 111 (now Chico-Leland Stanford Lodge No. I 1 I by consolidation).
M :.W:. Bro. Alexander was born in Chico, and attended the local
public schools. Our Grand Master entered the U.S. Navy immediately after
graduation from high school, and served as a hospital corpsman at various duty
stations.
Upon his return to Chico he enrolled at Chico State College (now Chico
State University), and graduated with a major in history, and a teaching credential.
His first teaching job was in Fortuna, but he and Greta soon returned to Chico,
where he taught for the remainder of his thirty-five years as an educator at Chico
Senior High School. He taught history and civics, and also spent some years as a
Vice Principal at the school. He retired in 1987, and devoted his time to his
family, his church, and to Freemasoruy. He is an active member of St. John's
Episcopal Church in Chi co, and has served in many leadership capacities,
including being a" licensed layreader.
Our Grand Master was often heard to say that there were four
cornerstones in his life: His family, his profession as an educator, his church, and
Freemasonry. And Freemasonry bcnefirted from his considerable talents as a
leader. A member of both the York and Scottish Rites, each equally honored him
for his service and devotion. He presided as High Priest of his Royal Arch Chapter,
Illustrious Master of his Council of Cryptic Masons, and Commander of his
Commandery of Knights Templar. He was awarded one of the highest honors in
York Rite Masonry, the York Cross of Honor, and later, as a result of his service
as Grand Master, he was elevated to the York Grand Cross of Honor. In the
Scottish Rite he was a 33rd Degree fnspector General Honorary, and a Past
Venerable Master of the Sacramento Lodge of Perfection. He also served other
Masonic bodies as a leader, and is a Past Sovereign of St. Francis Conclave of the
Red Cross of Constantine.

CHARLES H. ALEXANDER

appoi nted Grand Orator by M :.W:. Leo Mark, and he served on many
committees of Grand Lodge through the years . In 1992 he was elected as Junior
Grand Warden, and progressed through the chairs until he was Installed as (irand
Master of Masons in California on October 11 . 1995.

John Runcie, Master of Santa Clara Daylight Lodge. Under Dispensation. Gavels
used during this session of Grand Lodge were those presented to the Grand Master
on August 17, l 99 by I3ro. George McDonald of Nevada Lodge No. 13, and on

Officers Association.

Officers, entered the auditorium to the sound of trumpets and organ, and assumed
their stations. The Grand Chaplain gave the invocation.

E ULOGY
EDWARD HENRY SIEMS

Grand Master 1948 - 1949
Born: December 7, 1903
Entered into Rest: January 29, 1996
This is a eu logy for the Senior Past Grand Master of th is Grand Lodge.
who led the Past Grand Masters into this Grand Lodge each October for over two
decades. This is also a eu logy for the patriarch of our fam ily. Although, Edward
Henry Siems was the very essence of a Master Mason, one well worthy of imitation
as a leader, mentor and friend to countless men and women - he was for hi s family
primarily a loving, caring and devoted husband. father. grandfather and great
grandfather.
The family often joked about Ed as the only person we knew who would
wear a three piece suit and hat to a ball game or a picnic. And so he would - and
so he did with perfect dignity. elegance and distinction.
For nearly 30 years Ed lived across the street from this building where he
was surrounded by the chimes of Grace Cathedral, the clang of the California
Street Cable Cars and the discordant sounds of emergency vehicles and late night
car horns, tires and brakes . His wife Ginny had a home high in the mou ntai ns of
Hawaii where the dominate sound was silence - they natura lly divided their time
between the two homes. Year after year Ed would report that he couldn't sleep for
days after they sett led into the home in Hawaii. We wou ld - year after year fa ithfully ask "Why?" And wi th that famous, wonderful. warm sm ile he wo uld
reply. " Who can sleep with the chatter of those darn birds!"
Ed traveled extensively after his retirement in 1977 but his heart never left
San Francisco. Likewise his life-long devotion to Freemasonry never wavered .

EDW A RD H. SIE!\lS
P.\ ST GR\;\"!) M.-\ STER

December?, 1903-January29. 1996

Bro. Ed. our 83rd Grand Master. was born on December 7th 1903 in
11uena Park, California. He received his early schooling at Centralia Grammar
School (this school was rebuilt in 199..t and I had the privilege and pleasure as your
Grand Master to lay the cornerstone with Ed's older brother Ted in attendance).
EJ graduated from Anaheim Union High School and the University of California
at Berkeley in 1927.
Our Brother married Pauline Baker in 1933 and they had one son,
Frederick Armstrong, who married Dolores Hammond and they presented Ed with
fou r grandchildren: Michae l. Marilyn. Philip and Valerie. Following Paul ine's
death, Ed married Vi rgin ia Ah rendt. And following Frederick's death . Dolores
became my wife. There are three great grandchildren: Nicholas. Christopher and

PROCEEDl'.'-JGS OF THE

Most Worshipful Brother Siems served this Grand Lodge as Grand Master
from October 15, 1948 to October 14, 1949. He was Raised in Buena Park Lodge
No. 357 on February 14, 1929. His illustrious Masonic career included serving as
Master of Plymouth Lodge No. 560 in 1941 (now Orinda Lodge No. 494 ),
President of the East Bay Masters' and Wardens' Association in 1942, and
Inspector of the J4th Masonic District from 1943 to 1946. He served as Grand
Treasurer for five years. He served as a Trustee of the Masonic Homes of
California. and was Chairman of the Memorial Temple Building Committee which
was responsible for erecting this magnificent memorial home for our Grand Lodge
and the Masons of California. Later. he served four years as President of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board. He was elected Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge in 1960, and retired in 1977. He also served as President of the
Conference of Grand Secretaries of Grand Lodges in North America. He was a
member of the International Supreme Council of the Order of OeMolay. and a 33°
Mason in the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite.
Ed's business career included four years in stocks and bonds followed by
years with Key System Transit Lines as Secretary-Treasurer, Vicethree
twenty
President and Corporate Director and twenty-eight years as a Director and Trustee
of Olivet Memorial Park in Colma.
Our distinguished Brother·s civic and community service activities were
equally impressive. Ed was a forty-nine year member of Rotary. member and
Director of both the Junior and Senior Chamber of Commerce as well as the United
States Chamber. He served on the Alumni Council University of California. and
was a member of the Pacific Railway. the Athens Athletic. Commonwealth and
Bohemian Clubs.
Ed was an Elder and member of the Board of Trustees of the First
Presbyterian Church of Berkeley and an active member of Grace Cathedral San
Francisco. For his entire life. Ed had a firm religious foundation of belief and
practice. His friend, the Very Reverend Allen Jones, Dean of Grace Cathedral
spoke at his Masonic funeral.
Ed passed away at his San Francisco home on January 29th. 1996 and as
was his wish. the funeral service was conducted here in this building by Past Grand
Master. Donald B. Mccaw. acting as Master, and Most Worshipful Charles H.
Alexander, Grand Master, acting as Grand Chaplain.
It seems firting to conclude this Eulogy to the Grand Lodge by sharing a
portion of the Eulogy delivered on behalfof Ed's family on February 3rd, 1996:
"This morning's gathering of family and friends in loving memory of Ed
Siems is not, is not one of sadness but rather a gathering of celebration
and of joy. The joy of which we speak is both special and unique for it

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

13

is the joy of recalling how each of us shared in Ed's long. productive and
rich life. A life which spanned nearly a century from 1903 to 1996. Bv
any measure truly a full and rewarding life. Such a life needs to b~
acknowledged with joy for it was a life which renected a profound
celebration of life from the first day to the last
Ed Siems was just 18 years old when the then President of the United
States. William G. Harding, a Master Mason made this statement at a Masonic
cornerstone ceremony.
"There is nothing in Masonry that a free,
Religious and just American could not
be proud to subscribe to and be a
berter citizen for so doing."
We have no way of knowing whether our Ed ever heard of or much less
read that statement. But the record is clear. Ed 's entire adult life was a affirmation
of that stntement.
The biography in today' s program is an enduring and impressive record
of one who embraced his religion with all his heart, who subscribed to the teaching
of Freemasonry and then set about to be a ··berter citizen." That process also mad;
him a better son. brother. husband. father. grandfather. great grandfather and
friend.
One of Ed's greatest personal satisfactions was that his brother Ted (now
93) shared his Masonic experience. Ted served as Ed's Grand Sword Bearer in
l 948 and then served as a long time District Inspector in Southern California. And
also, that Ed was privileged as Grand Master to welcome his brother Charles into
the Masonic Fraternity.
Nearly twenty years ago the Grand Lodge of California in it's official
publication referred to Ed Siems as "The Consummate Mason", and so he was! I
personally doubt that there is a single activity of Masonry that Ed did not enrich
with. his willingness to serve during his 67 year membership. But of all of his
manifold areas of Masonic service including that of DeMolay, Scottish Rite, Grand
Treasurer. Grand Secretary, and Grand Master, he was most proud of his role in the
creation of this magnificent building atop Nob Hill.
Ed served as the chairman of the Buildino Committee and as first
President of the California Masonic Temple or Masonic Center.
. ~ven after Ed retired as Grand Secretary in 1977 he retained the keys to
.
this buildtng and rarely a day passed when he was in town that he did not visit th e

G RAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

3rd floor Grand Lodge Office and walk through from California Street to Pine and
from Pine Street to California. On the appropriate day of the week Ed's route
would include the San Francisco Bible Club, The Rotary Club, and an afternoon
of dominos at the Bohemian Club.
This building constructed of steel, concrete, marble and glass was much
more to Ed. It was the very symbol of Freemasonry in California - as it is today
and will be for generations to come. Ed's affection for this structure was no doubt
enhanced by the considerable challenge he faced in both raising funds and directing
the construction on this extremely difficult site.
In 1963, shortly after construction was completed, Ed moved across the
street to an apartment at 1200 California Street, reportedly to be near his Grand
Secretary's office on the third floor of this building. But I believe Ed wanted to be
able to look down on this building from his living room.

Ed ' s dear friend Ralph Head, Editor of the Californ ia Freemason in an
article shortly after Ed's retirement an Grand Secretary captured the essence of
Ed's life in a quotation from Cicero.
''In nothin g do men more nearly
approach the Gods than in doing
good to their fellow men."
Ed Siems' devotion to and love for his family and his chu rch and his
unequaled record of service to his community and to Freemasonry attest to his
w ill ingness to devote his time, abundant talent and inex haustible energy to '·doing
good" to and for his " fellow men ."
Ed always considered himself very fo rtunate in h av ing a loving and
d evoted family and a wide circle of friends. The truth is we were each and all
fortunate in ha ving Ed Siems share our lives!

EMMETT SHAW
Born: October 18, 1924
Entered into Rest: April 21, 1996

Emmett Shaw, born October 18, 1924, in Merced, California . Entered
into Rest, April 21, 1996. He was a member of Yount Lodge No. 12, having been
Raised to the Sublime Deg ree of Master Mason in that Lodge on May 29, 1984.
Brother Shaw was a man of great love for others, and great love for his
Fraternity. In 1994 when Grand Lodge began a search for an assistant to help our
Grand Organist with his duties in Northern California, Emmett's name was quickly
submitted by many who knew him, and his devotion to Freemasonry. When asked.
as always, Emmett said "yes!" As evidence of his devotion to Freemasonry in
general, and to his Lodge in particular, he was the recipient of the Hiram Award
from Yount Lodge No. 12 on May 24, 1994.
During the two years that Emmett served this Grand Lodge as Assistant
Grand Organist, he won the hearts o f those who knew him, and his devoted wife,
Maxine. It has been said that " a friend is only a stranger whom we have not yet
met." That saying wou ld typify Emmett. If he found you a stranger, he left you a
friend. And so it is that many, many friends now miss Emmett, for he wou ld not
let you be anything else other than his friend.
Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy resting place! Until then, dear
brother until then, farewell!

GRAND MASTER 'S MESSAG E
147TH ANNUA L COMMU NICATIO N

The California Masonic Code requires that the Grand Master shall present
at each Annual Communication, a message to the craft covering topics as required.
That is the task to which I address myself this morning

General Commen ts About the Grand Lodge Year
I wonder if other Grand Masters, as they have reached the end of their
tenn, have not been reminded, of a portion of the General Confessio n as found in
the older editions of the Book of Common Prayer, which says,
"I have done those things which I ought not to have done, and I have left
undone those things which I ought to have done ... ''
Yes, as I look back upon this past year, there are those things that I have
occasionally said, that I wish I had not said, and there are things that I have done
that I would not do again. I am sure that it would not be too hard to find things
that might have been done that would have been beneficial to the craft, that did not
get done. But yet, overall, I feel that I have been blessed by one of the greatest
experiences that one can imagine. I do not mean to say that it has all been pleasant.
Some of the prot11ems that come to your Grand Master are decidedly unpleasan t,
and makes one wonder how seriously some of our brethren take their obligation s.
However, there are few experiences in my life time that compare as far as
reward, feeling of accompli shment, brotherho od, and fellowship, with that of
having the opportunity to serve as your Grand Master. I thank you all most wannly
for having sufficient confidence in me to choose me to lead you for this past year.
The hospitalit y extended to Greta and me as we have traveled the length of our
great state, has been absolutel y great!
There is a strong possibility that the Grand Master is likely to get a
somewhat distorted picture of the state of the craft. He cannot visit more that just
a handful of the Lodges of the state. That is usually by invitation for some special
event that a Lodge has planned. Quite frequently a Grand Lodge Opening is a part
of the occasion. Enthusias m is high for these events . The brethren make special
efforts to get the membersh ip out and produce a quality event. If one were to make
an evaluation of the craft based only upon those Lodges which I have been invited
to visit, I would conclude that the craft is in excellent condition , the spirit is high,
and brotherho od and good will prevail. However, as well know, there are many
problems facing the craft today.

32

PROCEEDINGS 01-' THE

There is one particular aspect of being your Grand Master that has been
very heart warming that I would like to share with you. I refer to the duty of the
Grand Master to present seventy-five year pins to our brethren. I gave thirteen
such pins; another was presented by Past Grand Master Leo Mark. I wish to relate
to you one 75-year pin which was rather special. I got a call from a Secretary of
one of our Lodges, imploring me to arrange to award a 75 year pin as expediently
as possible. The brother had qualified some several months earlier, but it was
overlooked. We made the arrangements and met at the mobile home park where
he lived. Since we had little time to collect biographical material, I called on
several members of the family to comment on the life of our brother, and then I
called on him. He began speaking very deliberately,
"This reminds me of twenty-five years ago, when 1 got my fifty year pin.
It was really a nice evening. I was really enjoying myself. Everyone was
shaking my hand and wishing me well. Then someone told me I had to
say something. I was not prepared. And I am not prepared today. But,
if you will all promise to come back twenty-five years from now, when I
receive my hundred year pin, I promise that I will have a speech for you
then."
That is a great story! I particularly like that the optimism expressed in that
Jener, particularly when it is not too hard to find Masonic gloom and doom writers
who tells us the craft will virtually cease to exist by 2020.

I want to read an excerpt from a letter that I received from Worshipful J.
B. Settle, Master of Trinity Lodge No. 27, following the presentation of the
Seventy-five year pin:
"This presentation did much to enliven the entire hospital and has resulted
in starting the restoration procedure of an employee of the hospital who
had taken a dimit from another Lodge and now wishes to affiliate with
us."
That illustrates how important the various public ceremonies of our
fraternity can be, and how important it is that they be done proficiently and with
dignity. As a result of this one ceremony, a brother, once lost, is now found.
Yes. we can also hear stories of gloom, and predictions of doom. One of
the most common is the complaint that we have one, two, or several Past Masters
serving in the line ofour Lodges. Certainly one would concede that it is desirable
to have new blood in the line of all of our Lodges. But it is not an omen of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

33

fraternal disaster to have brethren serve more than once as Master of the Lodge.
Look to your history! As we go back into the early days of the fraternity in this
state, it is very common to find where one brother has served four, five, six,
perhaps as many as a dozen years, in the officer of Worshipful Master. lam sure
that he wearied at times, but why did he do it? He did it because to him it was a
moral imperative to keep alive the flame of Freemasonry in that community, a
flame that was in danger of flickering out. Perhaps, in these troubled times for our
country, in which the moral level of our society no longer seems in tune with the
principles and precepts of Freemason, we have a similar task to keep alive those
timeless, ageless, eternal values that are heart and soul of Freemasonry. Perhaps,
that is the task that the Great Architect of the Universe has assigned for us to do,
waiting when the day will come when once again our society is reflective of the
moral, social, and ethical values that Masons everywhere cherish. Let us, therefore
gird ourselves to the task before us, that when our sojourn on this earth is done, we
may receive from God the Father, that welcome plaudit, "Well done, thou good and
faithful servant."

Problems With Irresponsible Use of the Black Cube
However, just as our society seems to have lost its sense of direction and
purpose, evidence exists that brethren in our fraternity have forgotten some of the
teachings that were given them in our degrees . Letters come in to your Grand
Master that tell al! unpleasant side of the our fraternity. My brethren, while these
instances are rare, we do have bigotry hiding behind the black cube in some of our
Lodges, where, it is all too evident that race and ethnic background have been the
basis for rejection of candidates. One instance, after a minority candidate had been
rejected, a brother told the Master, giving it to him ''strictly in charee" that he had
cast the cube on the basis of the race of the applicant. Brethren, I wish I had the
answer to this problem, because if it continues to fester, it will inevitably bring well
deserved public condemnation down on us. This will not be the sort of thing that
we can dismiss as the raving of a religious fanatic, as we can some of the criticisms
of Masonry today, but will expose us, justifiably, to the charge of hypocrisy. The
critics will indict us with the charge, "You say that Masonry unites all good men
under the brotherhood of man and the Fatherhood of God, but your practice tells
us that racial and ethnic bigotry sometime prevail." A candidate for the degrees
of Masonry, if we believe what we say we believe, must be judged on the basis of
his character, on his reputation in the community, on his contributions to his
community, and never on prejudice based upon race, ethnic background, or
religious belief.
Can we overcome this by " whispering good counsel in our
brother's ear?" I sincerely hope so, because if we are to retain what many of us
value in Freemasonry, the requirement of unanimous consent for membership, then
that right must be exercised only within the restraints of justice. Our ritual tells us

34

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LOOOE OF CALIFORNIA

that "Justice is that standard or boundary of right that enables us to render unto
every man his just due without distinction." My brothers, we must both heed and
practice that admonition.

on these with you today. Last year, Grand Master William Stovall made some

Prince Hall Visitations
A more positive development in this area has been the heart wanning
reports that have been infonnally given to me, or which I have read about in the
trestleboard of the various Lodges, and in some case personally experienced,
regarding visitations to and from Lodges of our Prince Hall brethren. Universally,
the reports have indicated the most positive feelings about these visitations.
While. during the various meetings which took place leading up to the joint
recognition by the two Grand Lodge, I had met on an informal basis with many of
the Prince Hall Masons, it was not until July of 1995 that I fonnally met with our
Prince Hall brethren, when I addressed their Religious service and made some
remarks to that group. I reprinted those remarks in The California Freemason. I
had them reprinted not so much because I wanted you to know what I said, but
rather because it needed to be said to our members as well. True, as a result, I had
a couple of anonymous mailings of hate literature, but most rewarding was the
number of unsolicited letters and personal comments which I received endorsing
the sentiments expressed in that talk. After getting to know personally more of our
Prince Hall brethren, I have developed a suspicion that they may take a closer look
at those important factors of character, integrity, and morality than we do, when
judging the fitness of their applicants.

The label program and the mailings with the California Freemason were
not initiated by me. However, the pin program for the support of the Rose Parade
float was, so I shall address that first. I was concerned that the credibility of the
craft was at stake. We had celebrated the 75th Anniversary of the Order of
DeMolay, and the International Order of Job's Daughters by featuring these two
groups in our Rose Parade float. We were approaching the 75th Anniversary of
our third youth order, Rainbow for Girls, with the float in jeopardy. The Rose
Parade Committee had a smaller balance on hand than it had for several years. It
would be a real black eye for our fraternity to have to have said to our Rainbow
Girls-- "Sorry, we cannot do for you what we did for our other Youth Groups."
I was determined that should not happen. So, with the Chairman of the Rose Parade
Float Committee, Most Worshipful Stanley Channon, we began to investigate
means of augmenting and making more effective the fund raising for that project.
The Pin Program offered one distinct advantage, it would provide a contact with
every Mason of this jurisdiction. In short, this program was so successful that we
not only with have the funds to have a really excellent float on January 1, 1997,
featuring our Order of Rainbow Girls, but there will be some seed money to help
sponsor a float for 1998 celebrating the I OOth Anniversary of the Masonic Homes
of California. This does not diminish the need for continued voluntary
contributions , but it does take it out of the critical state that existed this time last
year.

I also had the experience, along with others of our Grand Lodge officers,
for the first time in the Masonic History of California, of visiting the tiled session
of the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of California, Inc., on July 14-16, at the Los Angeles Airport Hilton Hotel. Sixteen
of your Grand Lodge officers attended one or more sessions, with a substantial
number attending three days. It was a most interesting and historic event. And
today, we are, for the first time, welcoming our Prince Hall brethren to our Annual
Communicat ion. I hope that those Prince Hall brethren who are attending our
session here, will come away from our sessions with as positive a feeling as we all
had after attending their sessions.
Fund Raising Activities
I would like to comment on concerns expressed by some members of the
craft regarding various fund raising programs that have been employed. Some
members have taken offense at the label program that is used to support the
Masonic Model Student Assistance Program, the Pin program that was employed
· to give support to the Rose Parade Float, the inclusion of brochures in the mailing

Regarding the mailings with the California Freemason, with the inclusion
of these brochures. the sponsoring company pays the entire postage for that issue,
usually around $13,000. When you consider that the $1.16 per capita that is
allotted by your vote to the Freemason amounts to only 29 cents per issue, the
subsidy provided by these mailings enable us to continue the publication at the
same level, and at the same frequency, without asking for increased per capita. I
receive many Masonic publications from other states--many of which include
advertising. I would ask you, is the inclusion of an occasional brochure, which one
can discard if not interested, more offensive than filling a substantial portion of the
publication with advertising?

employed this same means of augmenting the financing of the their publications.
There may be as many as thirty jurisdictions involved in such programs, but for
these mentioned I have documentatio n.

Masonic Foundation, and it supports the Masonic Model Student Assistance

Program. Your response has been great, enabling us to maintain this program that
has elicited greater public approval than any program of recent memory.
Lastly, the credit card program. Virtually all of us use these plastic
conveniences from time to time. This program does not ask you to donate
anything, but simply gives you an opportunity, should you choose to do so, to use
a card that makes a contribution to the California Masonic Foundation when you
do use it. If you choose not to do so, then that is your choice. Although this
program came out over my signature, it was actually Grand Master William F.
Stovall who initiated the program. He did not rush into the program. He studied
the program for over a year. He contacted other Grand Lodges, of which there
were several, that were already using the program, asking them if they felt the
program was working, and if they were satisfied. He had the proposed contract
reviewed very carefully by the Chainnan of the Jurisprudence Committee before
making a commit-ment. How is it advantageous to us? The company, before
mailing one application, deposited $200,000 to the account of the California
Masonic Foundation. Future income is dependent upon the number who apply and
the extent of their usage.
I hope that I have, with these remarks, made these programs more
acceptable, or at least more tolerable, to those of you who have objections.
One Day Classes
I have, from time to time this year, received mailings extolling the virtue
of one-day classes to make Master Masons. A recent one of these came in booklet
fonn from the Imperial Shrine. Some of the.se one day classes have had the slogan.
.. All the way in one day," in which the class, in some cases numbering as many
as eight hundred, not only received the three degrees of the Blue Lodge, but also
the Scottish Rite or the York Rite and Shrine, all in one day. Some of the
supporters of these. short cuts to Masonry have argued that those who have been
made Masons in this manner have about the same level of active participation as
those who have followed the traditional course. The booklet sent out by the Shrine
has much statistical material about the educational level of the class members,
how many had annual incomes exceeding forty thousand dollars, the professional
standing of the members of the class, the age level of the candidates, and other
data. The one thing that I did not see in the publication was what percentage of
these huge classes stayed awake to witness the work. I have generally not
responded to such communications, because, unlike some other jurisdictions, the
Grand Master of California does not have the power, by edict, to suspend our law
or make new law. And frankly , my brethren, if as your Grand Master I had such
power, or were you to have granted me such authority, I would not have exercised
it to authorize one day classes in this jurisdiction. To me. it would be a basic

I

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

37

change from the traditional, individual, and very personal, process of one man
being "regularly and separately made a Mason." There is an individual relationship
of the brother to the Lodge and of the Lodge to the brother. That is much, much
different than the process of having a mass of bodies sitting on the sidelines
watching an exemplar go through the work.
I say this not because I feel it will be popular, as I know it w ill be
unpopular with some, but rather because it is my strong personal conviction that
to make radical changes in our fraternity by making Masons enmass, would change
the sense of individual responsibility that is basic to Free-masonry . To attempt to
gain members, by adopting the hurry up standards of a society that seems to have
lost its moral compass, would be a grave error. That which comes too easily ,
generally has little value to the person. St. Paul tells us, "Prove all things; hold fast
that which is good."
The day may come when the Grand Lodge of California with authorize
such classes, but if such should take place, it should be done only by vote of this
Grand Lodge, not by edict of a Grand Master.
Decisions and Recommendations:
The bulk of my decisions and recommendations have been previously
mailed to each of the Lodges, so you have all had the opportunity to read them. I
shall not list or discuss them at this time, but will defer comment at the time each
is presented before Grand Lodge for consideration.
Except when necessity
requires, it is desirable that the Decisions and Recommendations sent out to the
Lodges in advance. I have done so. However, there two additional issues which J
shall present to you at this time .
On September 7, 1996, the Grand Lodge of California Instituted Black
Mountain Lodge U. D. According to Section 14080 of the California Masonic
Code, such dispensation tenninates the first day of the month in which the next
succeeding Annual Communication is held. The same section further provides that
"if Grand Lodge orders the issuance of a charter, the dispensation shall be
revived ..." However, there is no provision in the present Code to provide for the
continuance of the dispensation until the next Ann ual Communication if a charter
is not granted. Obviously, the time between September 7 and October I is too
limited a time for Black Mountain Lodge U. D. to demonstrate its qualification to
receive a charter from this body.
The refore, it is my Recommendation N o. 8, that the dispensation issued
to Black Mountain Lodge U. D. be revived and continued in force until October 1,
1997. Since this action is not clearly specified in our Code, this will require a fivesixths vote to approve. It sha ll be ta ken up in the regular order of business.

which are not in anyway sectarian, but which speak profoun dly to
the task which

41

GOLDEN VETERANS AW ARDS

Our Father. by whose servants,
Our house was built of old,
Whose hand hath crowned her works,
With blessings manifold,
For thine unfailing mercies,
Far strewn along the way,
For all who passed before us,
We praise thy name today
The change-ful years unresting,
Their silent course have sped,
New comrades ever bringing,
In comrades steps to tread,
And some are long forgotten,
Long spent their hopes and fears,
Safe rest they in thy keeping,
Who changest not with years,
They reap not where they labored,
We reap what they have sown,
Our harvest may be garnered,
By ages yet unknown,
The days of old have dowered us,
With gifts beyond all praise,
Oh, Father make us faithful,
To serve the coming days.
Thank you.

All Masons can be proud of our Masonic Youth Orders. The Order of DeMolay: the
International Order of Job's Daughters: and the International Order of.Rainbow for Girls.. Thest three
or anizations have for at least seventy-five years provided positive influences on the lives o young
g nd women These organizations seek to teach character building traits l o thousands of young
\/\Mh so ~any forces in our society either neutral or even hostile to the development of poSlbve
behavior. the need 15 greater than ever for orgamzabons such as our Masonic Youth.

As perhaps the only Grand Maste r. at least in recent memory, to have been active in public
education in California, I perhaps have a greater interest in the Public Schools of Californ ia than most
members of the craft. In some respects the publtc schools of o ur state face a similar p roblem than our
fraternity faces Both are subject to irrational criticism by those with little knowledge of w hat they really
stand for, by people who make no effort to see the positive achievements. The schools of this state
have never before fa ced such challenges as they have over the last several decades, with l ~e rally
d ozens of different languages and dialects in the classrooms; a society that has grown i ncreasingly
violent and which tends t o reject many of the values assoctated with education; a society with an
mcreaS1ng percentage of chrldren from single parent families and homes wrth declining parental
interest in education.
I therefore urge a ll Masons of the State of California to redouble their efforts to aid a nd sup port
their public schools; to give their support to our Masonic Model Student Assistance Program to help
deal with the problem of drug and alcohol abuse: and above all, give their support to those dedicated
classroom teachers who are the vanguards of the educational strugg le that our society faces today

PROCLAMATION

For over one hundred years, the Masons of California have been dedicated supporters of the
Masonic Homes of Calfomia. This has resulted in our having two homes, both of which are regarded
as models of loving care and concern for distressed adults and unfortunate children. In recent years .
our Masonic charity has extended into the community. with the Non-Residence Assistance program
and Outreach Services, giving direct aid to Masons and widows to enable them to remain in their own
homes. Every Mason of this state can be truly proud of this great example of charity that comes from
the heart. Over and over again, I hear the residents of our home tell how grateful they are that they
can live out their lives in dignity, cared for by the love and watchful care of the brethren of California .

A f ew years ago: m ost of our_members of California Masonic Lodges wer e, at be st, only
vaguely aware of the California Masonic Foundation. However. rn recent years, this agency o f your
Grand Lodge has e_mbarked on some very vigorous programs- programs that not only serve our
society and our public school system . but enhance the public perception of Freemasonry we have
been able not on ly to increase our scholarship involvement, but have instituted a n exciting new
program: The Masonic Model Student Assistance Program. Many of the brethren have seen the tapes
that beautifully explain this p rogram

An important facet of the financial base of our California Masonic Homes is the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. For the past several years. the Masons of this state have consistently
contributed over one million dollars lo this fund. That sounds like a tot of money, but when you
consider that the total annual budget runs over IWenty million dollars. you can realize that we need lo
not only maintain that level of support. but increase ~ if possible.

As word of our Masonic Model _Student Assistance Progr am has spread across the craft, th ey
have responded With great generosity and have provided a financial base to con tinue the gre at
program No other Masomcally sponsored program in recent history has r eceived greater public
acceptance and a cclaim than has the Masonic Model Student Assistance Program. Who deserves
the credrt for this?_ The rank and file of the Masonic brethren of California who has re sponded most
ltberally to the vanous fund ra1S1ng programs, such as the mailing label program.

I therefore proclaim the month of May 1 996 to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

I could stress the need for your continuing support, however , most of all I wa nt to m ake this
proclamation a recognition for the great involvement of our b rethren.
I therefore proclaim the month of August 1996 to be

and urge the Master of every Lodge to redouble efforts to increase the level of participation in his
Lodge.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION MONTH

I direct that this Proclamation be read in every Lodge in this jurisdiction at the Stated Meeting
in February and March of 1996. and~ convenient, printed in the Lodge trestle board.

In considering a proclamation for observance of the signing of the Unrted States Constitubon
1n September of 1767. I am reminded of the words of a very eminent junst. Judge Learned Hand
speaking at ·1Am An American· Day ceremonies in 1~ In his remarks he cauboned that ·courts
laws, and coos11tutions." could not be the protector of freedom. • ...these are false hopes. Liberty lies
in the hearts of men and women, when rt dies there. no constitution , no law, no court can save rt; no
constitution, no law. no court can even do much to help it.'
So, while we as Masons revere and respect the Constitution. which has served our nation so
well. let us not forget that the Constitution cannot protect us from ourselves. It is the spark of liberty
in the heart of each Amencan that makes our Constitution work for the common good. Other nabons
have virtually copied our Constitution, bU1 their governments have failed , because the love of liberty
was lacking in the hearts and minds of their people . Let us therefore, as Masons and as Americans,
assume the responsibility of keeping tha1 spark of liberty alive in our country by recognizing that rt is that
sptrrt which makes the Constitubon work.
In that sptrit. I therefore proclaim the month of September 1996 to be
UNITED STATES CONSITTUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
and direct each Lodge of this JUlisd1ction to hold appropriate aciivities celebrabng the Constrtubon as
a document which will survive and serve America as long as the spirit of liberty lives m the hearts and

REPORT OF THE DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
1996-97 Grand Lodge Budget
Allen B. Gresham, Deputy Grand Master

The 1996 per capita of $ 16.11 assessed on the basis of 107, 131 Master
Masons is expected to produce a revenue of$1 ,725,880 (down $34,667 from the
prior year). Other miscellaneous income, including interest income and the
dividend from Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc., will result in a total estimated
income of$ 1,899,380.
The estimated expenses for 1996-97 are $1 ,468,961 , plus $ 128,557 for
publishing the California Freemason magazine. The difference between income
and total expenses is $301,862, and is allocated to Depreciation Reserve ($50,000),
and the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund ($251 ,862). The Grand Lodge Endowment
Fund was establ ished to help offset future declines in membership, th us help ing
soften the impact of the rapid decline in membership expected to continue over the
next few years. The Endowment Fund was established by vote of Grand Lodge to
smooth out future increases in per capita by reserving some present income for
future need.
Please note that expenses in the Proposed Budget for 1996-97 are less
than those in the approved Budget for 1995-96. For the past several years each
Grand Master has made a commitment to reduce the budget to reflect the decline
in membership. And Grand Lodge has voted to support this commitment by
increasing the per capita to offset inflationary costs. The decline in membership
results in less income both to individual Lodges and to Grand Lodge. The Grand
Lodge Budget reflects this reality each year by showing a reduction in
expenditures. The Proposed 1996-97 Budget is no different. We experienced a
5.74% decrease in the number of assessable members this past year, a number that
has been very much the same each year for the past several years. We project a
continued drop in membership of approximately 5% to 6% each year for the next
several years. The Proposed Budget represents a continuation of the concept of
"shared sacrifice" between our Lodges and Grand Lodge.
As yo ur Deputy Gnmd Master I pledge to you the contin uation of
responsible and prudent management of the resources of Grand Lodge in 1996-97.
Working together we can use our limited resources to strengthen Freemasonry in
California, while supporting programs important to our Lodges and to our
members. I am encouraged that many Lodges are beginning to see more
applications for membership, and a revived interest in Free masonry in their local
community. I firmly believe that we will see stronger and more active Lodges each
year. Your Grand Lodge is pledged to support that effort by using the financial
resources provided by our members wisely and well.

Lodge Budget for submission to Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication. That budget ts
prepared with the assistance of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance, and the Grand Treasurer. It is
based on the per capita adopted by G,-and Lodge at lhe previous Annual Communication, and collected
from each Lodge in accordance with the number of Master Masons carried on the rolls of the Lodge as
of June 30 nelCI preceding the forthcoming Annual Communication.
At the I 46th Annual
Communication in October, 1995, theper capita was established at $16. 11 (including Sl.16 for the
California Freemason magazine). As of June 30, I 996, our Lodges reported 109,853 Master Masons,
less 2,722 whose dues had been remitted. The net assessable membership 1s therefore 107,131 Master
Masons, and it is upon lhis figure that lhe 1996-97 Budget is based.

Memorandum from Depury Grand Master
August 16, I 996
Page 2
Please note that expenses in the Proposed Budget for 1996-97 are less than those in the approved
Budget for 1995-96. For the past several years each Grand Master has made a commitment to reduce
the budget to reflect the decline in membership. And Grand Lodge has voted to suppon this
commitment by increasing the per capita to offset inflationary costs. The decline in membership
results in less mcome both to individual Lodges and to Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge Budget
reflects this real1ry each year by showing a reduction in expenditures. The Proposed 1996-97 Budget
is no different. We experienced a 5.74% decrease in the number of assessable members this past year,
a number that has been very much the same each year for the past several years. We pro1ect a
continued drop in membe rship of approximately 5% to 6% each year for the next several years. The
Proposed Budget represents a continuation of the concept of "shared sacrifice" between our Lodges
and Grand Lodge.

As your Depury Grand Master I pledge to you the continuation of responsible and prudent management
of the resources of Grand Lodge in 1996-97. Working together we can use our limited resources to
strengthen Freemasonry in California, while supporting programs 1mponant to our Lodges and to our
members. I am encouraged that many Lodges are beginning to see more applications for membership,
and a revived interest in Freemasonry in their local commwiity. I firmly believe that we will see
stronger and more active Lodges each year. Your Grand Lodge is pledged to suppon that effort by
using the financial resources provided by our members wisely and well.
1997-98 Grand Lodge Per Capita

In accordance with the principles above, the 1996-97 Proposed Budget recommends that the per capita
for 1997 be established at S!6.77, which is a 4% increase. With mcome expected to drop by another
6% in 1997 from the continuing decrease in membership, this increase will allow us to suppon
programs important to our Lodges and to your Grand Lodge, while funding a lesser budget in 1997-98
than the current year. This continued reduction in expenses refl ects the realiry we face, while also
recognizing the reality of the need to support important programs and acti\1ties. The proposed 1997
per capita includes an amowit for the California Freemason magazine, our prime means for
communicating with all our members.

As you study the attached pages, please be reminded that the figures represent many hours of hard
work to bring you a responsible budget based on the best information possible. It represents a
commitment to prudently manage the resources of Grand Lodge now, and for the future. And it
represents my conunitment to you to conrinue to strengthen our beloved Fraternity by ensuring a sowid
financial base of operat10ns for your Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF THE SENIOR GRAND WARDEN

Per Capita Recommendations for 1997-98
Anthony P. "Tony" Wordlow, Senior Grand Warden

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Legislation adopted at our 1993 Annual Communication charges the
Deputy Grand Master with the preparation of a budget covering his anticipated year
as Grand Master. Preparation must begin during his year as Senior Grand Warden.
The Per Capita which you act upon at this Annual Communication will be for our
1997-98 Grand Lodge year. Preliminary work on the 1997-98 budget began several
months ago.
In the communication sent to your Lodges by our Deputy Grand Master,
you noted we are again supporting a 4% increase in lhe Per Capita for the 1997-98
year. Included allocations in the Per Capita are $1.20 per member for the
California Freemason and with postage increases already implemented and more
increases expected, lhis will probably not cover the total cost; and $1.18 allocated
for insurance coverage. If each lodge were to purchase this insurance
independently, the cost would be many times higher than $1.18, probably well over
$8.00 per member. This insurance covers members during lodge activities.
As stated in lhe Deputy Grand Master' s communication to you, our Grand
Lodge will again have a smaller operating revenue than for the previous year. Your
Executive Committee pledges itself to continue the concept of shared sacrifice.
Although the Per Capita increases, it will be matched, as it has been for the past
several years, by reductions in lhe operating costs of your Grand Lodge equal to lhe
revenue lost by declining membership. Careful oversight and tight control of all
Grand Lodge expenditures will accomplish our goal.
After consulting with members of the Grand Lodge Finance Committee,
who will present this to you for adoption in their report, we ask for a total Per
Capita for the 1997-98 Grand Lodge year of $16.77 of which $1.20 will be
allocated to the California Freemason and $1.18 to insurance.
The allocation for the California Freemason will probably not cover the
anticipated cost - with more increases in postage expected. It is likely we will need
to subsidize the California Freemason from operating revenue. This has already
been considered in the preliminary budget planning.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting to the
members of this Grand Lodge on the financial condition of Grand Lodge and its
entities, which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the California Masonic Foundation, and the Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc. (please refer to the opinion letters attached hereto by your
auditors).
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Public Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain a complete record of income and expenses for the
period.
The delegates to the Annual Communication are, in effect, the
stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge and you are encouraged, and it is
recommended, that you read and review this report. Your observations are
appreciated.
Both the Grand Lodge and each of its related entities are in sound
financial conditioA. The extent and size of our charitable activities were financially
possible in large measure due to the generosity of prior generations. To assure the
future of these fine programs we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial
support.
Respectfully submined,
Thomas C. Holm, Grand Treasurer

We conducted our audit in accordance \\ith generally accepted auditing standards Those standards require
that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements arc
free of material misstatement An audlt includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supponing the

principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall financial

In our opinion, such~onsolidated financial statements present fairly , in all material respects, the

of an operating lease with the Temple (see Note 6).

Functional Exp~nse Allocations - Expenses, such as depreciation and amortization, supplies, travel,
personnel and occupancy costs, are allocated among program services and general and adrninisLrative
expense classifications based on employee ratios and estimates m:ide by the Grand Lodge's management

Collections - The Grand Lodge owns a collection ofjewelry and other objects, most of which have
historical significanu. The jewelry collection is used in Lodge ceremonies, and the other objects are
displayed in the T emplc Museum. Purchases of collection items are reflected as decreases in unrcstncted
net assets in the year m which the items are acquired The Grand Lodge docs not recognize these assets as
contnbut1ons as they are protected and preserved, held for public exhibition, and are subject to an
organizational policy that requires proceeds from the sale of collection items to be used to acquire other
collection items. Accessions and dcaccessions during 1996 were not significant.
Deferred Per-Capita Rev~nu~ - Dues received for the subsequent fiscal year are recorded as deferred

The Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California :
We have audited the accompanying statement of financial position of Masonic Homes of California (a
California nonprofit corporation) as of June 30, 1996, and the related statements of activities and
changes in net assets and of cash flows for the year then ended. These fi nancial statements are the
responsib1licy of Masonic Homes of Cahforn1a management. Our responsibilicy is to express an opinion
on these financial statements based on our audic.
We conducted our audit in accordance "ith generally accq>ted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of matenal misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the
overall financial statement presentation We belie\'e that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our
opinion.

ln our opinion, such financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of
Masonic Homes of California as of June 30, 1996, and the results of its activities and changes in net
assets and its cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles.
As discussed in Note 1 to the financial statements, the Masonic Homes of California changed its method
of accounting for contnbutions received to conform with Statement of Financial Accounting Standards

No. 116.

ORGANI ZATION AND SUMMAR Y OF SIGNIFIC ANT ACCOUN TING

POLICIE S

Orga11hatio11 - Masonic Homes of California ("Masonic Homes'), a California
nonprofit corporation,
admmisters a home for adults at Uruon City, California, and a home for adults
and children at Covina.
California. The homes are supponed by The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of
California ("Grand Lodge') and members of the Masonic Fraternity in California.
The adult residents "'ho enter Masonic Homes are required by a hfe care agreement
to assign all their
assets to Masonic Homes in exch311gc for conunuing care for the remainder of
the resident's hfe In the
event that a continuing care contract is canceled by the resident through withdr:rwal
within the first ninety

NOTES TO THE FfNANCIAL ST ATEMENTS

5-8

We have audited the accompanying statement of financial position of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple (a California nonprofit corporation) as of June 30, 1996, and the related statements of acti\~ty
and changes in net assets and of cash flows for the year then ended. These financial sta.tements arc the
responsibility of the California Masonic Memorial Temple' s management. Our responsibility is to
eiqircss an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit.
We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accountmg principles used and significant estimates made by rnanasement, as well as evaluating the
overall financial statement presentation. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our
opinion.
In our opinion, such financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of
the California Masonic Memorial Temple as of June 30, 1996, and the changes in net assets and its cash
flows for the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
As discussed in Note 1 to the financial statements, the California Masonic Memorial Temple changed its
method of accounting for contributions received to confonn ,,.1th Statement of Financial Accounting
Standards No. 116.

Organii:.ation - The California Masonic Memorial Temple (the "Temple") is a nonprofit organization.

is to be transferred to either or both the Endowment Fund of Masonic Homes of California ("Masonic
Homes") and the California Masonic Foundation (the "Foundation"). The amount and proportions of
such income to be distributed is at the sole discretion of the Board of Trustees.

require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the

retirement age (65). For ser.1ce prior to January 1, 1993, !he annual retirement benefit at normal
retirement is equal to 2 % of the a verage annual compensation earned during the five calendar years prior
to January l, 1993 times years of service through 1992. For service after December 3 1, 1992 the annual
retirement benefit at normal retirement is equal to 2% of the compensation earned in each full and partial
year of service.

FUNDING POLI C Y
Prior to January 1, 1982, contributions to the P lan had been ma.de by participating employers and
employees based upon a percentage of covered payroll. Effective January I , l 982, th_e requirement for
employee contributions was terminated. The employers contnbute actuanally deternuned amounts _
sufficient to amortize the unfunded present value of accumulated plan benefits over the working l1fettme
of the active participants. The Plan met the minimum funding requirements of ERISA.

DESCRIPTION OF THE PLAN AND SUMMARY OF
SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Genual - The California Masonic Retirement Plan (the "Plan'') is a defined benefit plan that provides
retirement benefits for substantially all employees of Masonic Homes of California, Masonic Grand
Lodge and Component Organizations (collectively, "Grand Lodge") who have reached the age of2 1 and
completed one year of service. It is subject to the provisions of the Employee Retirement Income Security
Act of 1974 ("ERISA") . Participants should refer to the Plan documents for a mo re complete description
of the Plan.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRET ARY

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
My Brethren,
This is the fifth time that I have had the privilege of addressing you as
of this Grand Lodge. The 1995/96 Grand Lodge Year has been
Secretary
Grand
Grand Lodge Office, and this report will detail the activities of
your
for
one
a busy
the Grand Lodge Office on your behalf.
Membersh ip
The decline in membershi p continues to challenge your Grand Lodge
leadership, as well as the leadership of our constituent lodges. Last year I reported
that we had 116,531 Master Masons in this jurisdiction. As of June 30 of this year
we had 110,227 Master Masons. a loss of 6,304. This represents a 5.41 % decline.
We also Initiated 1,222 Entered Apprentice Masons. These new Masons, however,
do not show up as members until they become Master Masons. We Raised only
788 Master Masons in 1995/96, down from 1,020 new Master Masons in 1995.
This represents almost 23% fewer Master Masons Raised to the Sublime Degree
of Master Mason ihan were raised the previous year. By way of contrast, in 1995
we Raised 13% fewer Master Masons than we did in 1994. In other words, not
only is our actual membershi p decreasing, but the intlux of new members is
decreasing by a greater percentage each year.
It is difficult to calculate the number of Entered Apprentices who failed
to become Master Masons during the year, partly because our Lodges are active an
year long, and the statistical year may cut off the count in an arbitrary manner.
However, it is possible to calculate the ratio of Entered Apprentices to Master
Masons at any one time as somewhat of a measure of our ability to add to our
assessable membership rolls. At the end of the 1994/95 Grand Lodge Year the
nwnber of Entered Apprentices for the year was 24% greater than the number who
became Master Masons. In 1995/96 this percentage grew to 35%. Different
conclusion s may be drawn from these figures, but since the number of Entered
Apprentices in 1995 decreased over the number in 1994, it is fair to say that fewer
Entered Apprentices became Master Masons last year than in the previous year.
And since we count only Master Masons as full members for statistical purposes
at the Grand Lodge level, we continue to lose membershi p both at the beginning
and at the end of the journey. We have no control over deaths, but we do have
some control on how many new Master Masons we have each year.

178

179

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Leadership

My thanks go to all those who helped make this happen. The cooperation of an the
Lodges was noted and appreciated.

This last year the Grand Lodge Office expanded one of our major
leadership training programs in Grand Lodge. The Secretaries' Administrative
Workshops are designed to help Lodge Secretaries become more proficient in their
duties. In particular, they are designed to help strengthen the Lodge Leadership
Team headed by the Worshipful Master who is the chief executive officer of the
lodge. With the Secretary as the chief administrative officer, and the Treasurer as
the chief financial officer, Lodges can have a strong and effective leadership at the
top. Together with the Wardens, these elected leaders are able to shape the future
of the Lodge in an effective fashion . For some time now we have had the very
effective Wardens' Retreats as a part of our leadership training program. To this
we have now added the Secretaries' Administrative Workshops, which teach
Secretaries the supportive skills needed by the Master and Wardens. Six of these
were held in the spring, and each was very well attended. And in addition, a
training workshop was held for new Secretaries to help them cope with the difficult
learning of this most responsible position in the Lodge. More than 400 participants
took part in these seven workshops which were sponsored by the Grand Lodge
Office, and taught personally by the Grand Secretary and his Executive Assistant,
Joel Springer, along with the help of experienced Secretaries as presenters.

Secretaries' Associations
Secretaries' Associations continued to be a prime means of communication
for the Grand Secretary's Office. There are eight active associations in the
jurisdiction, with a new one added this year. They meet four times a year with the
Grand Secretary, or his representative, aiill afford a valuable foruin for the sharing
of ideas and the discussion of items of mutual interest. And they provide a
valuable link between the Lodges and the Grand Lodge Office.

Recognition of Other Grand Lodges
The Grand Lodge of California maintains fraternal relations with many
other Grand Lodges throughout the world. Of great importance during the past
Grand Lodge Year was the completion of mutual recognition between the Grand
Lodge of California and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii.
Both Grand Lodges entered into full fraternal relations effective February l, 1996.
Our Grand Master also received requests for recognition from other Grand
Lodges not presently recognized by the Grand Lodge of California. It is our
custom to follow the advice of the Commission on Recognition of the Conference
of Grand Masters of Masons in North America, and only one of these requests for
recognition is at present endorsed by the commission. Accordingly, recognition
was extended to the Grand Lodge of Senegal, in Africa, by Most Worshipful
Charles H. Alexander. A request to approve this recognition as pennanent will be
laid before Grand Lodge by the Grand Secretary at the 147th Annual
Communication.
Thanks
Finally it is important to extend thanks to Most Worshipful Charles H.
1
Alexander, Grand Master, for his continued support for the Grand Lodge Office,
and his unfailing encouragement to the Grand Lodge Office staff. It was a pleasure
to serve under his leadership, and my report as Grand Secretary is their opportunity
to express their gratitude as well.
Respectfully submitted,

Membership Database

John L. Cooper III, PM

The biggest achievement of the year was the reconciliation of the Grand
Lodge Office Membership Database with the individual Lodge records. A
tremendous effort was made to bring the Grand Lodge Office Database into line
with Lodge records, and through the hard work of all the Secretaries, together with
the Grand Lodge Office staff, this was accomplished. By June 30, 1996, more than
96% of the Lodges reported that their records agreed with Grand Lodge with a
variance of no more than a few members. And most of the others reported only
minor variances. The accuracy of the infonnation in the database is essential to the
quality of reports prepared by the Grand Lodge Office, not the least of which are
the eligibility lists for those who ire to receive fifty year and seventy five year pins.

209

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER

Most Worshipful and Brethren:
Since our last Communication another 365 days has been added to the
annals of this Grand Lodge, and I thank you for permitting me to be a part of its
illustrious history by serving as its Grand Lecturer.
Performance without hesitation to maintain accuracy and excellence of our
ritual is, and will always be, our strongest resolve.
As we traveled throughout the jurisdiction, we found far too many of our
Lodges are struggling to exist because of a lack of officers to staff them . But of
course, our shrinking membership by another 6,500 and 11 Lodges less doesn' t
help. Nevertheless, we are most grateful to those tenacious brethren who refuse to
say "Let's forget it''.
During the year 19 seminars were conducted from one end of the
jurisdiction to the other. With the exception of two, all were very well attended.
In closing, my personal thanks to our Grand Master and his wife, Greta,
for all the courtesies extended to me throughout the year, along with the warm th of
their friendship. To the rest of the "team" who have acquitted themselves so ab ly
in our ceremonies and for their everlasting friendship, thank you.
To our Candidates' and Officers' Coaches, your efforts are deeply
appreciated. To (jur Inspectors and to those who have left us during the year, no
expression of gratitude can be adequate.
To our Grand Secretary and his entire staff for their valuable assistance,
thank you.
To my colleagues on the committee who try to cover all the bases
throughout the jurisdiction all the time, my sincerest thank you.
Finally, and reluctantly and regretable, we say good-bye to one of our
esteemed colleagues - Worshipful George Anderson, Assistant Grand Lecturer for
Division IV. George has asked not to be reappointed in order that he and his wife,
Sue, might have the opportunity to pursue some of their goals that have eluded
them for so long. George, a grateful Fraternity and we your colleagues, salute,
embrace and thank you for your dedication and devoted service. We wish for you
and Sue, God speed, may your respite be a most enjoyable one and that you will
return to the "vineyards" as soon as possible. God Bless, and thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand Lecturer

GRANO CHAPLA IN'S MESSAG E

" Look Up and See the Banners Flying"
A Homily for the Vesper Service
l47'h Annual Commun ication
Grand Lodge of F.& A.M. o f California
The Rev. William Bowler Jefferies
Retired Clergy Member
Californi a Nevada Annual Conferen ce
The United Methodist C hurch
October 13, 1996
Let us pray:
Let the words of my mouth
And the meditations of our hearts
Be acceptabl e in Thy sight.
0 Lord. our rock and our Redeemer.
--adapted from Psalm 19: 14
During the darkest days of the Battle of Britain, when the aircraft of the
Gennan Luftwaffe.made their nightly visits to the skies above England, when the
air-raid sirens wailed and dwellings and other property exploded or were consumed
by names. when families were forced to interrupt their nonnal nocturnal routines
and accept confinem ent in stuffy undergrou nd shelters, when sudden death or
dreadful injury could befall those caught above ground during the rainstonn of
bombs and missiles, a series of articles appeared in a British magazine called The
Guardian . These articles, written by a professor at the University of Oxford, were.
when collected into a book, destined to become some of the most widely read
devotiona l or re ligious literature of the twentieth century, and their author, Clive
Staples Lewis, known almost exclusive ly by his initials, C.S. Lewis, became
perhaps the best know interprete r of traditional Christianity of our time, at least the
best known Christian theologia n who never bore the charisma, or the burden, of
being ordained.
Oddly enough, the war-time book by C.S. Lewis, called The Screwtap e
Letters, did not deal directly with the terrifying suffering the British people were
then undergoin g. Instead, it dealt with the personal struggle every r ighteous
person, in whatever clime or period of history, must wage in o rder to (to put it in
Masonic tenns) " circumscribe his desires and keep his passions with in due bounds
towards all mankind ..." Perhaps it was as though this reminder of the constant

215

PROCEEDINGS OF TH E

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

interior banle for right living tended to minimize the colossal exterior battle with
Nazi bombs and terrorist propaganda and rendered it less overwhelming.
The Screwtape Letters is an allegory, a fonn of literature familiar to
Masons, and is not intended to be taken as reality. It purports to be a series of
letters of advice from a devil down in Hell, named Screwtape, to his young
nephew, a tempter called Wormwood, at work on his very first " case" up here on
earth . At one point in his advice-giving, Screwtape gives Wormwood this caution
regarding the "care" of his " patient" : " Never let him look up and see the banners
flying."
Screwtape, or rather C.S. Lewis, was right. The Devil can do his most
efficient work amongst us when we fail to "look up and see the banner flying".
Another Christian allegorist, the Puritan John Bunyan, writing in the seventeenth
cenrury, in his work The Pilgrim's Progress, places one of his characters directly
outside the walls of the celestial city. He has a muckrake in his hand, and is
perpetually looking down and stirring up the mess of corruption at his feet. He is
so occupied with observing the muck that he never looks up to see the shining
alabaster walls rising above him.

worldwide and history-long scale, quite possibly the most famous, the best known
piece of art connected w ith the Masonic fraternity is a grand opera, a piece called
Die Zauberjlote, "The Magic Flute" composed by Masonic Brother Wolfgang
Amadeus Mozart in Vienna, Austria in 1791.

214

The shepherd psalmist, "the sweet singer oflsrael", realized the necessity
of looking up and seeing the banners flying. In the Sixtieth Psalm, identified in its
Hebrew introduction as "a golden poem of David for teaching", Israel's second
king uttered this prayer for his people at a time when their fortunes seemed to be
ebbing:
0 God, Thou hast cast us off,
Thou hast scattered us,
Thou hast been displeased:
0 tum Thyself to us again.
Thou hast showed Thy people hard things,
Thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment.
Yet Thou has given a banner to them that fear Thee,
That it may be displayed because of the truth.
--Psalm 60: I, 3-4
As we contemplate the future of our beloved fraternity this week, as we
make decisions affecting its fate in the twenty-first century, let us not forget to look
up and see the banners flying.
In this regard, let me impart to you a piece of Masonic advice which is
over two hundred years old. For those brethren who are convinced that "real men
don't eat quiche" nor listen to Classical music, I have shocking news: On a

It is universally conceded that Mozart' s music for this opera is far superior
to its story line, its libretto, wh ich was written by Mozart's Masonic Brother, a
minor actor, baritone, and impresario named Emanuel Schikaneder; nevertheless,
the libretto is supposed to reveal some of the arcane teachings of Masonry. So
much so, in fact, that during the nineteenth century the false rumor got started that
Mozart's early death, at age thirty-five and only two months after the first
performance of Die Zauberjlote, was caused by his Masonic brothers incensed by
his revelation of their secrets. I don ' t have to tell you, of course, that th is theory
is pure canard, if for no other reason than that the libretto of the opera was not
written by Mozart, but by Schikaneder, who lived on into the next cenrury
unharmed by any imaginary Masonic "hit men" .
Discovering the Masonic conte nt of Die Zauberjlote has been, for me, a
project of long-standing duration. You might even say it has been nearly life-long,
if you trace the beginning of my Masonic life bac k to my Raising in Chico Lodge
No. 11 I forty-five years ago this month. Some thirty-five years ago, while I was
teaching in Glendora and attending Graduate School at Claremont, I learned of an
outdoor performance of "The Magic Flute" in English out in Redlands. So I drove
out there to attepd it, but I am afraid that I came away more confused than
enlightened.
Since then I have learned a little German, have read several books on the
life of Mozart and his connection with Freemasonry, and have watched or listened
to several other performances of the opera. (The circumstances of my life as a rural
person have caused most of my attendance at dramatic performances to be via radio
or television.) And I think that I may have found a key which may unlock the
myste ries of"The Magic Flute".
One would logically assume that the bulk of the Masonic teaching in the
p lay could be found in the dialogue assigned to the characte r of Serastro, the high
priest of the mythical temple of Isis and Osiris. The role is sung by a bass, for
profundity ' s sake, and was supposedly modeled after the Worshipful Ignaz von
Born, the Master of the Lodge which Mozart and Schikaneder attended in Vienna.
But as sometimes happens to men who have had the honor of presiding over a
Lodge, Serastro's attempts at educating his fellows are hindered by his ponderous
sense of self worth.
No. What authentic Masonic lore which can be found in Die Zauberjlote
is, in the main, confined to the words and actions of three mag ical boys sent to aid

216

217

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the young hero of the opera, Tamino, in going through the initiatory ordeals he has
to face .

And, my brothers and sisters, I submit that what is true of biological
creatures of connective fiber and tissue, of chromosomes and DNA, is also true of
institutions like Freemasonry.
A recent issue of the National Geographic magazine carried an interesting
article concerning the newest discoveries regarding the supposedly extinct species
of dinosaurs. Heretofore, scientists have thought that the nearest living relatives
of these prehistoric beasts were cold-blooded reptiles, ugly, repulsive creatures like
homed toads and iguanas. In fact, the very name of the species, dinosaurs, means
in Greek "terrible lizard''. But palaeontologists are now finding evidence that
dinosaurs may have been warm-blooded, with hollow bones and an avian-like body
structure. In other words, dinosaurs may not have become extinct at all. We may
have them among us today; except we call them - - ~!
So may it be with Freemasonry as we move into the twenty-first century.
Possibly we are evolving into a more beautiful, more ethereal structure, nearer to
that heavenly Lodge whose order and beauty we all yearn for. " Look up and see
the banners flying!"

In good productions of Die Zauberjlote, these parts are acted by boy
sopranos. The staff in charge of casting and wardrobe try to see to it that they
resemble youthful Renaissance angels like those painted by Boticelli or Rafael.
. Good boy sopranos are very scarce, especially in today's society. (There
were st_ill a few Castrati around in Mozart's day!) For this reason, cheaper
productmns of the opera use female vocalists, a substitution which rather stretches
the imagination, the anatomy of the average operatic coloratura being what it is.
In Act One of the opera, these boys are described as "sch6n, hold und
weise", thus representing the three goals of Masonic aspiration, perfect Be,auty,
Strength, and Wisdom. Later on, Tamino pledges:
Die Weisheitlehre dieser Knaben
Sei ewig mir ins Herz gegraben.
Which I translate as :
The teaching which these lads impart
Be forever etched within my heart.
The point which these historic musical collaborators and Freemasons seem
to. be trying to tell us across two centuries of time is that the future of Masonry lies
with the young or at least with those who have young ideas.
We should not be frightened by change. Change is the means by which
th~ Great Artificer of the Universe works its continuing process of Creation. In
this sense then we are indeed in the eighth day of Creation as God continues to
perfect His cosmos, His natural order, through the processes of natural selection
and evolution, as Saint Paul so eloquently points out in the eighth chapter of his
Epistle to the Romans:
We. know that the whole creation has been groaning together in travail
until now ... For the creation was not subject to futility, not of its own
will but by the will of Him who subjected it in hope; because the creation
itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and obtain the glorious
liberty of the children of God.

As vanguard of the modern Masonic movement, and bearers of its banner,
we here today recognize that to be a real Mason is to be a better man in every
relation of life - a more considerate, loyal, and loving husband, a more devoted
father, a more involved citizen, and a truer friend. How then do we convey this

Remember the generous and compassionate veteran in the vineyards of

In the Odyssey, Homer informs us that Odysseus appointed Mentor, the teacher.
