There is a mentoring program based on consideration, respect, and
cooperation presently in use in other Grand Lodge Jurisdictions. It is a team effort
aimed at developing each brother to his fullest potential. This continuing
curriculum of support through mentor counseling, fraternal visitations, and Lodge
participation could be the stimulant some of our newly raised brothers need to stay
active after the Third Degree. Could your Lodge make use of such a program?
Then, contact your Grand Lodge Education Committee or the Masonic
Service Association of the United States about this formal mentoring program. It
consists of the Master of the Lodge assigning each candidate a well-informed
brother, knowledgeable in the Art of the Craft, to act as his mentor, educator, and
companion for a year. The mentor can either be assigned upon receipt of the
petition, or upon election of the candidate. He will contact the candidate and
advise him and his Masonic friends of his upcoming degree dates at the Lodge.
The mentor will assist the candidate throughout his degree work, but he
need not necessarily be his coach. However, he may be part of your Lodge's
Masonic Education Committee. Above all it is essential that he become imbued
with the spirit of the Fraternity and accept its purposes. ideals, and tenets as his
own, prompting the mentor to properly pilot the new Mason into this Grand Order
of Brothers and Friends.
The candidate meets with the mentor for a minimum of five one-hour
sessions. Beginning before the First Degree, and continuing between the three

GRAND MASTER'S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Decision No. 1
Application for Affiliation
on
Balloting
In 1995, Section 26120 of the Code was amended making optional the
investigation of applicants for affiliation. I was asked whether an petition for
affiliation could be presented and voted upon at the same Stated Meeting if an
investigation were not required because no objection were voiced at or before that
Stated Meeting.
At his installation, the Master assents to the following:
You admit that no person can be regularly made a Mason in, or
admitted a member of, any regular Lodge, without previous
notice, and due inquiry into his character.
While the 1995 legislation may have made optional the requirement of "due
inquiry", it did not alter the requirement of "previous notice." If a petition fo r
affiliation is read and voted upon at the same Stated Meeting, it fails to fulfi ll the
requirement of "previous notice".
It was therefore my decision that, even if an investigation were not
required, an application for affiliation must be voted upon no sooner than the next
Stated Meeting after it has been read in open Lodge. If there are objections, this
will allow time for them to be made.

If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master's
interpretative decisions are recorded:

At his installation, the Master assents to the following:
You admit that no person can be regularly made a Mason in, or

While Section 26120 of the Code may make optional the requirement of "due
inquiry" into the character of an applicant for affiliation, it does not alter the
requirement of "previous notice." If a petition for affiliation is read and voted upon
at the same Stated Meeting, it fails to fulfill the requirement of "previous notice".
Therefore, even if an investigation is not required because no objection has been
. made, an application for affiliation must be voted upon no sooner than the next

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master' s Decision No. 1 proposes to clarify the voting
requirements of a Lodge on a petition for " Affiliation" .
Legislation adopted at the 1995 Annual Communication eliminated the
requirement for investigations on Masons applying for Affiliation unless there is
an objection by a Brother. Section 26120 titled "Investigating Committee" does
not address the time necessary between the reading and the balloting upon an
application for affiliation.
This decision defines the tenn "Due Notice" and does not pennit a Lodge
to read and ballot on an application at the same meeting. A petition must be read
and then held over to the next Stated Meeting before being voted upon.
This Decision is consistent with Grand Lodge policy.

231

I was asked whether it is an appropriate use of Lodge funds to the pay the
service club dues of members of the Lodge. The portion of the California Masonic
Code most closely on point would be Section 21090 which pennits a Lodge to
expend not more than thirty percent of its total revenue for the purposes of
refreshments and the promotion of fraternal intercourse, including community
improvement.
I have heard of Lodges purchasing a membership in the local Chamber of
Commerce which in my view our law allows. Use of Lodge funds to pay Chamber
of Commerce dues involves "community improvement, charitable activity, or
sponsorship of programs that will benefit residents of the community in which the
Lodge is located" as permitted by Section 21090 of the Code. However, a
Chamber of Commerce membership is different from a service club membership.
A service club membership would seem to be more beneficial to the member of the
Lodge participating in the club's meetings while a Chamber of Commerce
membership would seem to be more beneficial to the Lodge. The support for the
community which Chamber membership implies would seem to me to be the
primary purpose for belonging, rather than the contacts which those participating
in it might receive. There is also a significant cost difference between the two
memberships. It ~as therefore my decision that Lodge funds may not be expended
to pay the service club dues of members of the Lodge. ·
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master's
interpretative decisions are recorded:
Interpretation of Section 21090 or the California Masonic Code.
Use of Lodge Funds to Pay Dues in Community Organizations
(1996 G.M. Decision No. 3)
Section 21090 of the Code penn its a Lodge to expend not more than thirty
percent of its total revenue for the purposes of refreshments and the promotion of
fraternal intercourse, including community improvement. A Lodge may therefore
become a member of the local Chamber of Commerce and pay the associated dues.
Use of Lodge funds to pay Chamber of Commerce dues involves "community
improvement, charitable activity, or sponsorship of programs that will benefit

However, a Chamber of Commerce membership is different from a service

Lodge, a service club membership is more beneficial to the member of the Lodge
participating in the club's meetings while a Chamber of Commerce membership is
more beneficial to the Lodge. The support for the community which Chamber
membership implies would be the primary purpose for belonging, rather than the
contacts which those participating in it might receive. There is also a significant
cost difference between the two memberships. Therefore, Lodge funds may not be
expended to pay the service club dues of members of the Lodge.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master' s Decision No. 2 responds to an inquiry from a Lodge
Secretary as to whether or not Section 21090 of the California Masonic Code,
which authorizes expenditures of Lodge funds for community activities, permits
the payment of individual memberships in civic or service organizations. The
Decision determines that while Section 21090 permits institutional memberships,
such as a Lodge's membership in the local Chamber of Commerce, it does not
reasonably include individual memberships or fees. The Grand Master believes
that a Lodge's membership in the local Chamber of Commerce is a proper
expenditure of Lodge funds under Section 21090 of our California Masonic Code
because the expenditure does involve, "community improvement, charitable
activity, or sponsorship of programs that will benefit residents of the community
in which the Lodge is located." He believes individual memberships in service
clubs are more beneficial to the individual than to the Lodge.
This Decision is consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.
Decision ADOPTED.

Decision No. 3
Advertising for Gambling in Masonic Publications
During the year, I was asked whether a Masonic Organization may accept
advertising from an Indian Gaming Casino in the Organization's official
pub Iication .
Section 15090 of the California Masonic Code reads in part as follows:

233

It seems to me that the acceptance of advertising in a Masonic publication for a
gambling enterprise (whether a legal or an illegal gambling enterprise) gives the aid
and countenance of Masonry to that enterprise. Because the receipts of that
gambling enterprise would pay for the advertising, the conduct of that gambling
enterprise has provided a monetary benefit to the Masonic publisher. It was
therefore my decision that the proposed advertising was not permitted by the Code.
Such advertising would not be permitted in a Lodge publication either.

If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master's
interpretative decisions are recorded:

Interpretation of Section 15090 of the California Masonic Code.
Advertisine for Gambline Establishments in Masonic Publicati?ns
0996 G.M. Decision No. 4)
The acceptance of advertising in a Masonic publication for a gambling
enterprise (whether a legal or an illegal gambling enterprise) gives the aid and
countenance of Masonry to that enterprise. Because the receipts of that gambling
enterprise would pay for the advertising, the conduct of that gambling enterprise
has provided a monetary benefit to the Masonic publisher. Accordingly, neither
a Lodge nor a Masonic Organization may accept advertising in its publications
from an gambling enterprise.
In addition, the following paragraph would be added to that portion of the
advertising guidelines applicable to Masonic Lodges which are found in that
appendix:

enterprise) gives the aid and countenance of Masonry to that
enterprise. Because the receipts of that gambling enterprise

The Grand Master received an inquiry from a Masonic organization
asking if it was permissible to accept advertising from an Indian casino.
The Grand Master' s Decision was that Section 15090 states that Masonic
organizations may not "profit directly or indirectly from any gambling enterprise."
Inasmuch as the advertising fees would be paid from the profits of the casino, that
would be indirect profit and prohibited by Section 15090.
This Decision is consistent with the policy of Grand Lodge.

Decision No. 4
Wearing Yarmulkes at Masonic Funerals

It has been a long standing practice at Masonic funerals of Jewish brethren
for each man in attendance, whether or not a Mason, to wear a yarmulke which for
Jews is an emblem of their faith. No problems related to this practice has ever
come to the attention of your Grand Master.
On May 14th of this year, I received a letter from a brother informing me
that he had been told by the District Inspector at a School of Instruction of a change

It is therefore my decision that the long standing practice of permitting the
wearing of yarmu lkes at Masonic services for our Jewish brethren may not be
restricted or impeded without legislation to the contrary adopted by this Grand
Lodge.

If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in wh ich the Grand Master's
interpretative decisions are recorded:
Interpretation or Section 28040 or the California Masonic Code.
Wearing Yarmulkes at Masonic Funerals

(1996 G.M. Decision No. 4)
Nothing in our Masonic law prohibits the wearing of yarmulkes at
Masonic funeral services.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Alexander, in this Decision, overruled a directive from the
Ritual Committee that no Mason attending a Masonic funeral for a Jewish Brother
would be allowed to wear both a Masonic Apron and a yarmulke.
In the text of the Masonic Funeral Service, page 7, the Master is instructed
to wear an evergreen, but is directed not to wear a hat nor wield a gavel. On page
8, all other Masons are directed to wear only a white apron, not any other more
embellished ones or other official regalia or emblems of authority. The rationale
for this instruction is that, at any funeral, there is only one authority, the Supreme
Being. Presumably it was this instruction that led to the directive that a Mason not
be permitted to wear both a yarmulke and an apron.
As an absolute condition for membership, Masonry requires an indi vidual
man to believe in a Supreme Being. Beyond that stated belief, however, Masonry
makes no restrictions with regard to what practices or customs that ind ividual

236

237

PROCEEDINGS Of THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

employs to express that belief. In fact, Masonry respects each individual religious
pursuit. By way of example, Sections 430 and 16080 of the California Masonic
Code limit the types of Masonic communications or acti vities which Grand Lodge
or a Blue Lodge can hold on a Sunday, in deference to the Sabbath observance of
many Christians.

It does not say to assemble as Christians or as kfil or as Muslims or as
Buddhists or as Adherents to any Reli~ion ; but in the ''Character of Masons".
The raiment of a "Mason" in all our ceremonies, whether in closed Lodge,
in procession or in open public ceremony, is the apron appropriate to rank. The
only head covering is that worn by the presiding officer.
The only exception to this rule is our Funeral Service when no head
covering is worn by anyone and the only apron worn is the white apron.

Furthennore, Masonry had steadfastly maintained that it is not a religion,
and that it is not in competition with any religious system. Section 380 of the
California Masonic Code prohibits Grand Lodge or any constituent Lodge from
interfering or voicing an opinion with regard to religious matters.
The wearing of a yarmulke is a Jewish religious custom. In that religious
pursuit, the yarmulke is a sign of respect to the Supreme Being, and it is a practice
that is expected from fill men who attend any Jewish religious function , including
Jewish funerals. The wearing of a Masonic apron at the funeral of a brother Mason
is a Masonic custom. It is a demonstration of the love and brotherhood which we
all feel toward each other, including the departed brother.
Clearly, there are Masons who are Jewish, and each of them will,
eventually, have the need for a funeral which will include elements of both Jewish
and Masonic traditions. At that time, other Masons will certainly want to be in
attendance. By compelling these Masons to choose which symbol to wear, we are
telling all Masons, and the rest of the world, that Masonry will not respect a
particular religious practice. Such an act would function ally interfere with a
religious matter, in violation of Section 380. Furthermore, the symbolic separation
of yarmulke and apron is a statement that Masonry and Judaism are in conflict.
The wearing of both a yarmulke and a Masonic apron at a Jewish
brother's funeral is certainly consistent with our policy and general purposes.
Report ofthe Committee on Ritual:

It is regrettable that at the eleventh hour of this Grand Lodge year that I
find myself at odds with our Grand Master's Decision No. 4.
This action was prompted by a Brother who disagreed with the guidelines
for conducting our Funeral Ceremony, guidelines that have been in place for years.
Lest we be misquoted, or lest our position be misunderstood, permit me
to review it with you.
The first paragraph of our service begins as follows:

In some cases when the ceremony takes place at a location outside of the
Lodge, our service may either precede or follow another service which may be
reli~ious or of another organization. During these " non-Masonic" ceremonies, a
Brother who is clad in a white apron may don a head covering which may include
a Yarmulke. As the Masonic ceremony has either not yet begun or has already
been completed, this wearing of a head covering would not be considered an
endorsement of any remarks a member of the clergy might make. Everyone
understands that our ceremony has either not yet begun or is over. But while the
"Masonic Service" is in progress, the only appropriate raiment is that of a white
apron with no head covering.
Freemasonry is not a religion. We have taken great pains over the years
to make that abundantly clear. Not is it a substitute for religion. It advocates no
sectarian faith or practice. As a fraternity we believe that the relationship between
the individual and his God is personal, private and sacred. Given this, we must not
give the appearance of any endorsement of a particular faith or creed, but leave that
to the individual outside of our ceremonies.
Beyond the particular case from which this issue was raised, if and once
we make an exception to this departure from our ritual, should we not permit
members of our concordant and appendant bodies to wear the head covering
representative of their organization and which may be equally as important to
them? For example, the "Fez" of Shrine, or the "Chapeau" of the Knights Templar,
or the "Fez" of a Sciot, or the cap of the Scottish Rite Mason.
We must remember, my brethren, that whenever and wherever we
assemble in the character of Masons, that the raiment of a Master Mason is and
must always be apron only.
My brethren, you cannot and must not allow this Decision to prevail.
Decision ADOPTED.

"Brethren and friends, it has been a custom among the fraternity of Free
and Accepted Masons, from time immemorial, at the request of a departed
Brother or his family, to assemble in the "character of Masons" ..."

Recommendation No. I
Establishes Rules for Joint Masonic Publications
During the year, I was asked to comment on the advertising rules
applicable to joint publications of Lodges and other Masonic Organizations. One
successful Masonic publication in this state is sponsored by and mailed to the
members of several local Lodges, several Eastern Star Chapters, the York Rite
Bodies, the Shrine Club, the Scottish Rite Club and the Masonic Youth Orders.
Due to rising costs, we can expect this format to grow in popularity. It is also an
excellent way to foster harmony among the members of the Family of Freemasonry
in a single community. Unfortunately, our law would seem to limit the permitted
advertisers in such a bulletin to the members of the Lodges involved and their
businesses. Members of the other participating organizations would not be
permitted to advertise. This limitation did not seem fair to me.
The Grand Master may authorize a Lodge to participate in any fund
raising activity (including trestleboard advertising) which is not otherwise
prohibited by our law. Accordingly, I initiated a pilot program this year to permit
advertising in joint Masonic publications by the members of any of the
participating organizations. Advertising was permitted only from persons
belonging to one of the participating Masonic organizations, with all advertising
income in excess of publication costs being donated to a recognized Masonic
charity. Any publication costs in excess of advertising income were shared
proportionately by the participating organizations, although our Masonic Youth
Orders could include material in the publication without charge. This pilot
program has worked well, and I recommend that you make it permanent.

Guidelines Applicable to Masonic Lodges.
Our California Masonic Code permits Masonic Lodges
to accept advertising in Lodge publications under limited
circumstances. These Guidelines answer many of the questions
which may arise in connection with that advertising. If a
question arises which is not adequately answered by these
Guidelines, Section 27600 of the California Masonic Code
should be consulted. If questions remain, then the Grand Lodge
Committee on Jurisprudence should be contacted .
A Masonic Lodge may pennit advertising only in Lodge
publications. This includes any publication which the Lodge
uses to communicate with its members. A Masonic Lodge may
therefore accept advertising for its monthly bulletin or
trestleboard. It may also accept advertising for its Lodge Roster
and installation programs. It may not accept advertising which
will not be printed in a Lodge publication. For example,
comme;cial advertising material cannot be posted in the Masonic
hall.
Except as noted below, advertising may be accepted
only from the Lodge's members and from businesses or
commercial establishments owned or operated by its members.
Advertising may not be accepted from members of another
Lodge. Advertising may not be accepted from the wife or other
relatives of a member. Advertising may be accepted from a
business only if a member of the Lodge has an equity or other
ownership interest in the business or holds an operating or
managing position in the business.
If the publication is jointly sponsored with another
Lodge or with the Eastern Star, York Rite or other Masonic
Organizations, advertising may be accepted only from a
sponsor's members and from businesses or commercial
establishments owned or operated by a sponsor's members. If

bulletin to all of their members, all of those members and their

Recommendation No. 2

Establishes Offices ofAssistant Grand Organist
and Assistant Grand Tiler
We have had, for several years, a brother who has regularly substituted for
the Grand Organist and a brother who has regularly substituted for the Grand Tiler.
In recent years, both the Grand Organist and the Grand Tiler have lived in the
South. Therefore , their assistants were selected from the North and regularly
substituted when Grand Lodge openings were held in the North. Use of these
substitutes has saved Grand Lodge money because it has reduced the travel
expenses necessary to bring the regular officer to events in the North. However ,
these brothers have on those occasions perfonne d all the duties of these offices
without any status or title that is really deserving of their effons.
I therefore recomme nd that we correct this situation by fonnally
establishing two new Grand Lodge offices: Assistant Grand Organist and Assist.ant
Grand Tiler. If you adopt this legislation , the Grand Master would be required to
appoint each assistant from the opposite part of the state from the regular officer.

§3140. GRAND TILER.
It shall be the duty of the Grand Tiler to:

Guard the outer door of the Grand Lodge and communicate with
the Grand Pursuivant;

Report to the Grand Pursuivant all applications for admission
and see that all who enter are duly authorized and properly

Make suitable preparation for the accommodation of Grand

Serve all notices and summonses, and perform such other duties
as may be required of him by Grand Lodge or the Grand Master.

The Grand Master may appoint an Assistant Grand Tiler from the
opposite part of the state from the Grand Tiler. The Assistant Grand Tiler
shall discharge the duties of the Grand Tiler in the absence of that officer.

In order to relieve some of the time and travel commitments of the men
occupying these two offices, Grand Lodge has, unofficially, identified counterparts
who live in the other part of the state. Thus, if the Grand Tiler or Grand Organist
reside in the South, another man who has the capability to substitute for him is
available in the North. The actual responsibility undertaken by each man is thereby
limited to a smaller geographical area. Furthermore, Grand Lodge has been able
to save money because of the reduced travel expenses.
We have now had several years experience with this system, and it has
worked very well. Grand Master Alexander is simply seeking to codify this system
formally.
The reco!llmendation is consistent with Grand Lodge policy and purpose.

Recomm endation No. 4
Establishes New Procedure for Change of Lodge Name
Under our Californi a Masonic Code, only Grand Lodge may change the
name of a Lodge, with one exception noted later. Accordin gly, a resolution must
be submitted, debate held and a vote taken. While a name change resolution is not
presented every year, they do appear periodically as Lodges resulting from prior
consolida tions reconside r the name previously chosen . In addition to being time
consumin g, the rule is illogical. A Lodge may change its name without Grand
Lodge consent when it consolida tes but cannot change its name without Grand
Lodge consent in any other circumstance.
I recomme nd that a Lodge be allowed to change its name following a
procedur e similar to that used when it amends its Bylaws. However , the Lodge
would not be pennitted to select a name already being used by another Lodge.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 14090 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended as marked and a new Section 14095 will be added
to the California Masonic Code to read as follows:

Recommendation No. 5
Warden in Preferring Masonic Charges
Junior
of
Modifies Duties
An unfortunate circumstance arose this year which caused me to reflect
on our rules regarding Masonic charges and trials. Under our law, the Junior
Warden is only required to prefer Masonic charges when both of the following
have occurred: (I) he has all of the facts required to show him that a brother is
guilty ofunmasonic conduct and (2) no one else brings the Masonic charges within
the next thirty days.· He is not obligated to bring Masonic charges ifthe facts in his
opinion are insufficient. He is under no duty to make an investigation to discover
further facts ifthe facts presented to him are insufficient to show him that a brother
is guilty ofunmasonic conduct .
In my view, the Junior Warden should have the duty to investigate further
when preliminary but not conclusive facts of unmasonic conduct are presented to
him. I also believe that our law would be improved ifthe Junior Warden were
required only to have reasonable cause to believe the brother to be guilty of
unmasonic conduct before preferring Masonic charges. At present, it would appear
that the Junior Warden must have no doubt of the guilt.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 32060 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended as marked:

§32060. CHARGES.
A charge or charges ofunmasonic conduct may be preferred against any
member of a Lodge or any Mason residing within the Jurisdiction of a

252

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodge by any Master Mason in good standing. All charges shall be in
writing over the signature of the accuser.
Charges to be preferred upon the Grand Master, as Grand Master, or a
Master, as Master, shall be preferred as provided for elsewhere in this
Code.

rf facts, from any source, are brought to the attention of the Junior
Warden of a Lodge showing that any Mason, over whom his Lodge has
jurisdiction,~ to be guilty ofunmasonic conduct, it shall be the duty
of the Junior Warden to investigate whether these facts and any other
facts discovered in the investi~ation ~ive reasonable cause to believe that
the Mason is ~uilty ofunmasonic conduct. and-ilf, for the period of 30
days following the completion of his investi~ation b1 ingit1g of !ttch fact!
to hi5 attention, no Master Mason in good standing has preferred charges
against such Mason and if the Junior Warden has reasonable cause to
believe that the Mason js ~ujlty of unmasonic conduct, then it shall
become the official duty of the Junior Warden to prefer the charges. He
does so as a Master Mason and remains the accuser throughout the
proceedings.
If the Junior Warden is the accused, or the information is against the
Junior Warden, it shall be the official duty of the Senior Warden to prefer
such charges.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master' s Recommendation No. 5 seeks to clarify the role of
the Junior Warden in the filing of charges. Problems have arisen in the past from
the language of Section 32060 of the California Masonic Code which requires the
Junior Warden to file charges when facts come to his attention showing a member
"to be guilty of unmasonic conduct". The Grand Master proposes to change the
phrase, "to be guilty of unmasonic conduct" to that of giving, "reasonable cause to
believe that the Mason is guilty of unmasonic conduct" . The Grand Master's
recommendation also would modify the Junior Warden's duty to provide that
where facts are brought to his attention showing that any Mason could be guilty of
unmasonic conduct, it will be his duty to investigate. If any of the facts previously
known or discovered give him reasonable cause to believe that the Mason is guilty
of unmasonic conduct, then it shall become his official duty to prefer the charges.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

253

This language reflects more clearly the intent of this section, and the role
most brethren perceive to be that of the Junior Warden.
The recommendation is consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
Grand Master Alexander's Recommendation No. 5 which has been
referred to your Trial Review Committee proposes an amendment to Section 32060
of the California Masonic Code to impose on Junior Wardens an affirmative duty
under specified circumstances, to investigate and prefer charges against a brother
for alleged unmasonic conduct.
Your committee believes that the amendment proposed by our Grand
Master would clarify a possible ambiguity which may now exist in the Code. Since
any amendment to the Code which clarifies an ambiguity will be beneficial to the
Craft, your Committee on Trial Review recommends a "Yes" vote.
Recommendation ADOPTED.
Recommendation No. 6
Permits Change of Time for Stated Meetings
It is my tecommendation that we amend the Uniform Code of By-Laws
to permit Lodges to hold their Stated Meetings at different times during certain
months of the year, if they choose to do so. We already permit Lodges to hold a
Stated Meeting on different days wh en they conflict with holidays or the Annual
Communication. It seems illogical not to permit Lodges some latitude so they
might vary the hour of the Stated Meeting by a similar procedure.
The reasons for this recommendation are three fold. One, the Grand
Secretary and the Inspectors constantly receive requests to make a time change, and
they have no choice but to report that there is no provision in our law to accomplish
such a purpose, other than a permanent By-Law amendment for each and every
Stated Meeting. Secondly, many Lodges are seeking ways to increase interest and
attendance at Stated Meetings. With the advancing age of our members, some
Lodges have desired to have one or more Stated Meetings at a different hour. They
cannot do this at present without changing the hour of all their Stated Meetings.
Lastly, many of our members, either by choice, or on medical advice, no longer
drive at night. During Daylight Saving Time, it would be possible to schedule
Stated Meetings at an earlier hour so that the business could be concluded and the
brethren on their way home during daylight hours.

254

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodges, by following the carefully proscribed procedure for amending
their By-Laws, should have this option.
We should also provide the means by which the Lodge, by majority vote,
could request a dispensation from the Inspector to allow a one time change of the
hour of a Stated Meeting. The Inspector already has the power to grant a change
of date. Why not also the hour?
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 4030 of the California Masonic
Code will be amended as marked:

Recommendation No. 8
Continues the Dispensation ofBlack Mountain lodge, U.d.

CARRY-OVER LEGISLATION

On September 7th of this year, Grand Lodge instituted Black Mountain
Lodge, U.D. According to Section 14080 of the California Masonic Code, this
dispensation terminates the first day of the month in which the next succeeding
Annual Communication is held. The same section provides that "[i]fthe Grand
Lodge orders the issuance of a Charter, the Dispensation shall be revived ... ".
However, there is no provision in the current Code for the continuance of the
dispensation until the next Annual Communication ifthe charter is not granted.
Obviously, the time period since September 7th is too limited for Black
Mountain Lodge to demonstrate its qualification to receive a charter from this
body.
I therefore recommend that the dispensation granted to Black Mountain
Lodge, U.D. be revived at the close of this Annual Communication.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

recommended that a charter be granted, as has the Committee on Charters. It is
therefore my recommendation as Grand Master that a charter be granted.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

1995 ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Grand Master Stovall's Recommendation No. S
Permits Licensed Caterers to Serve and Sell
Alcoholic Beverages at lodge Events
At the 1989 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge adopted more
liberal rules with respect to the use of alcoholic beverages at the activities of
Lodges and Masonic Organizations and by other groups when on Masonic
property. In 1990 and again in 1993, the Grand Master promulgated Guidelines to
help Lodges and Masonic Organizations interpret these rules.
We have now had five years experience with these rules, and one of them
has proven bothersome. Under Section 15050 of our Code, Lodges, Temple
Associations and other Masonic Organizations may rent or lease their land or
buildings to non-Masonic tenants other than business establishments who serve
alcohol ic beverages, if alcoholic beverages are not sold. Under this rule, you may
rent your building for a wedding reception or similar activity where alcoholic
beverages will be served but may not be sold by the sponsor or caterer, even if the
sponsor or caterer is properly licensed to sell drinks. In addition, Lodges, Temple
Associations and other Masonic Organizations may not have catered events on
Masonic property where alcoholic beverages are sold by the caterer, even if the
caterer is properly licensed.
It does not seem to me that these restrictions are required by the spirit of
the 1989 legislation. I therefore recommend that licensed caterers be permitted to
serve and sell alcoholic beverages at all Masonic events and at non-Masonic events
held on Masonic property, if all applicable California laws are followed. I also
recommend that you be permitted to rent your building to non-Masonic tenants for
a wedding reception or similar activity where alcoholic beverages may be served,
consumed and sold by the sponsor, if the sponsor is properly licensed.
Finally, I propose that Section 15050 be rewritten to make it easier to
follow than the current version of it.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section I 5050 of the California
Masonic Code will be repealed and replaced with the following:

260

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

§15050. ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES.
Alcoholic beverages may be sold, served, and consumed on
property owned by or leased to a Masonic Lodge, Temple
Association, or Masonic Organization and at Masonic activities
held elsewhere if the following requirements are observed:
A.

Alcoholic beverages may not be sold, served, or
consumed in a Lodge room or in a room in which
Masonic ceremonies are normally conducted except
when such room serves a dual purpose as a ceremonial
room and social room;

B.

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not maintain. on a regular or
permanent basis, a bar stocked with alcoholic
beverages;

C.

The funds ofa Masonic Lodge or Temple Association
may not be used to purchase alcoholic beverages;

D.

Alcoholic beverages may not be served, consumed, or
sold during the course of a meeting of a Masonic
Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic Organization;

E.

A Masonic Lodge or Temple Association may not
directly or indirectly apply for, assume title to, or
operate under any government license or pennit for the
purpose of consuming, serving or selling alcoholic
beverages, whether in, on, or away from premises
owned, leased, or rented by either of them;

F.

G.

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not rent or lease property in which it
has an ownership interest to business establishments
wherein alcoholic beverages are served, consumed or
sold unless such service, consumption, and sale are
incident to and not the primary purpose of the business;
and
Any sale, service, or consumption of alcoholic
beverages pursuant to this section must comply with all
applicable laws of the State of California.

If you approve this recommendation, the following alcoholic beverage
guidelines will replace those now found in the appendix of the California Masonic
Code in which Grand Master's interpretative decisions are recorded:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GUIDELINES FOR USE OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES
BY MASONIC LODGES AND MASON IC ORGANIZATIONS
Questions frequently arise with respect to permissible
use of alcoholic beverages in Lodge halls, on other property
owned by or leased to a Masonic body and at Masonic activities
held elsewhere. These guidelines explain the Grand Lodge rules
applicable to such use. These guidelines apply to Lodges,
Temple Associations, the Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the
Shrine, Eastern Star and all other prerequisite organizations and
their Temple Associations.
These guidelines address only the policy and
regulations of the Grand Lodge. Your use of alcoholic
beverages also must comply with the applicable Jaws of the State
of California and the rules established by your Masonic Temple
Association or other landlord.
A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association and other
Masonic Organization may allow alcoholic beverages to be
served on Masonic property to their members and invited guests,
with one exception. Alcoholic beverages are not permitted in the
room where a Lodge or a Masonic Organization meets unless
that rOOJll is also the regular social hall.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organi:rations may maintain a bar on Masonic property so long
as alcoholic beverages are not regularly or permanently stored in
the bar. Alcohol should not be stored elsewhere on Masonic
property either.
Lodges and Temple Associations may not use funds
from the Lodge's or the Temple Association's treasury to
purchase alcoholic beverages. However, funds collected by a
committee of the Lodge for social purposes are not Lodge funds.
Therefore, if a committee of the Lodge plans a Lodge activity
where alcoholic beverages are served, the committee may use the
money collected from ticket sales to purchase alcoholic
beverages. The excess ticket sale proceeds may not be given to
the Lodge until after the reimbursement has been made. No
Lodge or Temple Association funds may be used to reimburse
anyone who has purchased alcoholic beverages.
These
restrictions apply only to Lodges and Temple Associations. The
Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the Shrine, Eastern Star and

261

262

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

other Masonic Organizations may reimburse the purchase of
alcoholic beverages from their treasuries, if their regulations so
permit.
Alcoholic beverages may not be served, consumed, or
sold during the course of a meeting of a Masonic Lodge, Temple
Association, or Masonic Organization. Any alcoholic beverages
must be removed from the meeting room prior to beginning the
meeting. The meeting may be opened and called to refreshment,
after which alcoholic beverages may be served, but the alcoholic
beverages must be removed from the meeting room prior to
calling back to labor.
Lodges and Masonic Organizations may hold tiled
meetings and social events on non-Masonic properties where
there is a pennanent bar, such as a hotel or restaurant, provided
that no alcoholic beverages are present during any meeting. Any
bar located elsewhere in the building may remain open during
the meeting.
Licensed caterers are permitted to serve and sell
alcoholic beverages at all Masonic events held by any Lodge,
Temple Association or Masonic Organization on or away from
Masonic property, if aJI applicable California laws are followed .
No Lodge or Temple Association may directly or
indirectly apply for, assume title to or operate under any
governmental license or pennit for the purpose of consuming.
serving or selling alcoholic beverages, whether in, on or away
from premises owned, leased or rented by a Masonic Lodge or
Temple Association . Therefore, if alcoholic beverages are not
sold and served by a licensed caterer, there are certain
restrictions on the event which must be observed because the
event has not been licensed. As a general rule, no license or
pennit is required if alcoholic beverages are not sold and the
premises are not open to the general public when alcoholic
beverages are being served or consumed.
•

If alcoholic beverages cannot be sold, you cannot have
a cash bar or sell drink tickets or tokens to be
exchanged for alcoholic beverages. You may charge
for the meal or other event at which alcoholic
beverages are served, so long as everyone pays the
same price, regardless of whether they will be served
an alcoholic beverage. Alternatively, members and

GRAND LOOOE OF CALIFORNIA

guests may bring their own alcohol if alcoholic
beverages are not sold.
•

Under no circumstances may the general public be
present when alcoholic beverages are served without a
license. You may not advertise to the general public an

Masonic property. Only members of the sponsoring
Masonic body and their invited guests may be in
attendance when alcoholic beverages are served on
Masonic property by someone other than a licensed
caterer. The term "general public" does not include the
members of the organization, their families or friends.
If alcoholic beverages are not sold and served by a
licensed caterer, Masonic Organizations are subject to these
same restrictions unless the group is properly licensed by the
California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control. This may
include a single event license as well as a permanent club
license. Masonic Organizations, such as the Scottish Rite, the
York Rite bodies, the Shrine and Eastern Star, may hold such
licenses even though a Lodge and Temple Association may not.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organi?4ltions may rent or lease their land or buildings to
business establishments which serve and sell alcoholic beverages
as an incidental part of their businesses. For example, you may
rent to a restaurant which has a bar or to a grocery store that sells
alcoholic beverages. However, you may not rent to a bar
business or a liquor store, even those bars and liquor stores with
incidental sales of non-alcoholic products.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organizations may rent or lease their land or buildings to nonMasonic tenants otber than business establishments who serve
and sell alcoholic beverages, ifthe sponsor or caterer is properly
licensed by the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage
Control. For example, you may rent your building for a wedding
reception or similar activity where alcoholic beverages will be
served and sold by a licensed sponsor or caterer.
As a reminder, activities of a Lodge, Temple
Association or Masonic Organization are always subject to
Grand Lodge rules on commercialism and permitted financial
support, in addition to these guidelines.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
At the 1989 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge adopted more
liberal rules with respect to the use of alcoholic beverages at the activities of
Lodges and Masonic organizations and by other groups when on Masonic property.
In 1990 and again in 1993, the Grand Master promulgated guidelines to help
Lodges and Masonic organiz.ations to interpret the se rules. We have now had five
years experience with these rules, and one of them has proven bothersome. To
resolve this difficulty, as well as to consolidate the guidelines. Grand Master
Stovall recommended that Section 15050 of the California Masonic Code be
rewritten to permit licensed caterers to serve and sell alcoholic beverages.
This recommendation is consistent with current Grand Lodge purposes.

Report of the Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation:
Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation finds that Grand
Master Stovall's Recommendation No. 5 adequately restates current California
Masonic Code and Guidelines concerning the use of alcoholic beverages.

Too often, good men are denied admission to Masonry because one biased
or angry member objects. Most of us probably know of at least one instance where
an applicant was rejected for no valid and Masonic reason. We have considered
this problem in the past but have not yet found the appropriate solution. We
considered a three black cube proposal but many believed that this would only
encourage a malcontent to recruit two more objectors. We cannot solve the
problem unless the Lodge can discuss dispassionately the cause of the objection but
we have been reluctant to require a Mason to divulge his reasons for objecting to
an applicant's election.
I propose that we adopt an approach to the problem which is already in
our law. If an objection is made to the advancement of an Entered Apprentice or
a Fellow Craft, the Master appoints a committee to investigate the objection and
report to the Lodge. The Lodge then determines by a two-thirds vote whether the
objection to advancement is valid and Masonic. If two-thirds vote to advance the
man despite the objection, he advances. Otherwise, he does not advance.

The recommendation breaks new ground by its broadening of the Code 's
current definition of acceptable tenants, whose sales of alcoholic beverages are
incidental to and not the primary purpose of their businesses. The Code now
accepts only permanent tenants. Should the recommendation be approved, the
Code would then accept short-term, transitory tenants, whose sales of alcoholic
beverages are, also, incidental to and not the primary purpose of their businesses.

I propose that we adopt the same procedure for objections made before
initiation. If an objection is made to the Master before a man's initiation or if one
or more black cubes appear in the ballot box, the Master would appoint a
committee to inv~stigate the objection . While the committee would be available
to hear and discuss the cause of any objection, no one would be required to present
his objections to the committee. After its investigation of any sources available to
it, the committee would report to the Lodge. The Lodge would consider the report
and then vote on whether the objection is valid and Mason ic. If two-thirds vote to
elect the man despite the objection, he is elected. Otherwise, he stands rejected.

In addition, such transitory tenants would also, as a result of this
recomme ndation, be a llowed to serve and sell alcoholic beverages at most Masonic
events, if a ll applicable California laws are followed.

I believe that this approach will protect innocent applicants from rejection
for improper reasons yet protect the anonymity of those who choose not to come
forward with reasons for their objections.

The recommendation retains the current prohibition that a Masonic Lodge
or its Temple Association may not, themselves, sell alcoholic beverages to their
members or the general public.

26230, 26240, 26250, 26260 and 26270 of the California Masonic Code will be
amended and a new Section 26245 will be added to the Code as marked:

The Committee appointed to resolve any objection before

oral statements made shall be taken down in narrative or other
form by the Secretary or. at the Master's option. by a

further time be given by the Master or the Lodge. stating fullv
the cause of objection and its conclusions thereon. The
statements upon which the report is based shall be read in the
Lodge. if reguired. After receiving the report from the
Committee appointed to resolve the objection. the Lodge shall
vote by ballot on whether or not the objection is valid and
Masonic.
If in the opinion of two-thirds of the members present. the
objection is not a valid and Masonic one. the applicant shall be
elected without further ballot. The Master shall not allow the
same objection to be made a second time. The decision is final
and may not be reconsidered and no appeal may be taken. If the
objection is found to be valid and Masonic. the applicant stands
rejected and a reballot cannot. thereafter. be had on the same
application without obtaining a dispensation.

Recommendation NOT ADOPTED.
Grand Master Stovall's Recommendation No. 8
Modifies Prohibition on Bingo
At last year's Annual Communication, you approved Grand Master
Blomseth's recommendation for the appointment o f a special committee to study
our prohibition on bingo. The study would include a survey of Lodge interest in
changing our rules so long as our activities did not violate California law.
California prohibits b ingo when played as a game of chance for prizes, except
when conducted by cenain groups. California does not proh ibit bingo when you
wager nothing for the right to play.
The study committee was appointed and conducted the required survey.
Many of those surveyed objected to the use of bingo as a fund-raising activity but
interest was expressed in the use of bingo as a purely social activity. The study
committee has proposed certain changes in this area which are the basis of th is
recommendation.
If you adopt this recommendation, a Lodge or Masonic Organization will
be pennitted to sponsor bingo games as a purely social activity. Participation must
be limited to our members, their families and friends. The general public may not
be invited. There may be no signs or other advertising visible to the general public
referring to the game. There must be no charge for the opportunity to play. You
may not require a donation, admission fee, meal purchase or other charge for a
bingo card. Prizes of minimal value may be awarded to winners and may be
purchased by the sponsor or donated.

This new approach extends the procedure currently in place for objections
raised after an election for the degrees of Masonry to apply also to any instance in
which an unexpected anonymous objection, in the fonn of one or more black
cubes, occurs at the time of balloting. In the event that such a ballot occurs, the
Master of the Lodge must appoint a committee to investigate such an objection.
After the investigation of any and all sources available to it regarding the applicant,
including anonymous statements, the committee would report to the Lodge. A twothirds vote by the lodge would determine whether the objection is valid and, if not,
the applicant would continue despite the objection.

I believe that this recommendation will permit bingo for purely social
purposes without any violation of California law.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution 95-17

California Masonic Code Section 15090 includes Bingo as a gambling
enterprise.
Grand Master Stovall's Recommendation No. 8 would allow a Lodge or
Masonic organization to permit Bingo for purely social purposes when nothing is
wagered for the right to play.
This recommendation is consistent with Grand Lodge purposes.

Report of the Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation:
Freemasons in California have always prohibited Bingo Games in their
Temples when played as a game of chance. At the 1977 Annual Communication,
Bingo Games were specifically prohibited in the gambling section of the California
Masonic Code. This simple, unambiguous language effectively prohibited playing
of any type of Bingo Game, including those conducted when players wagered
nothing for their right to play Bingo as a parlor game.
The 1994 Annual Communication approved the Grand Master's
Recommendation for the appointment of a special committee to study this blanket
prohibition of all types of Bingo Games.
The intent of Recommendation No. 8 is to permit Bingo Games to be
played in a Masonic Temple only ifnot played as a wagering game of chance. By
the proposed language, participation in Bingo Games would be limited to lodge
members, their families and friends. The general public would not be invited and
no signage or advertising to the general public would be allowed to reference any
Bingo Game. No charge, donation, admission fee or meal charge would be
assessed for the opportunity to play. Prizes of minimal value could be awarded to
winners and could be purchased by the sponsor or donated to it.
Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation believes that Grand
Master Stovall's Recommendation No. 8 will adequately establish for the Craft a
definition of Bingo Games that are not wagering games of chance. However, this
revision of the unambiguous language of the 1991 Code revision will, in the last
sub-paragraph of the proposed CMC Section 15095, leave a certain ambiguity as
to the definition of"prizes of minimal value". For example: may there be monetary
as well as non-monetary prizes and what is the upper range definition of a minimal
amount?
We suggest that, should this carry-over legislation be approved, a further
effort be made to define acceptable, minimal prizes.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

Resolution 96-04

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of the Resolution seek to permit Lodges to purchase a life
membership for Golden Veterans' A ward recipients due to the fact that nearly all
The
of them are retired and living on fixed and usually reduced incomes.
proponents contend that some of these men may have difficulty in paying their
Lodge dues.
This resolution would add to Section 21080-C permission for a Lodge to
purchase a life membership for a Golden Veteran Award recipient.
Since it is already possible for a Lodge to purchase such a membership for
a retiring Worshipful Master, this proposal merely represents an extension of an
already-established Grand Lodge policy. However, one of the general purposes of
Masonry is a life-long committment to the suppo rt of a Lodge; if any member is
unable to pay his dues, there are already mechanisms in place and available to him
(dues remission). Hence, having a Lodge purchase a life membership for any of
its members is actually not consistent with the purposes of Masonry .

WHEREAS, there is a desire to reduce confusion at the opening of the
Lodge presently caused by the distribution of Officers' Jewels by the Master;
WHEREAS, there is no distribution of the Officers' Jewels at the opening
of Grand Lodge, but an entrance process of the officers instead; and
WHEREAS, such a procession by Lodge Officers would lend dignity to
the opening ritual of the Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Opening Ritual of the
Lodge be modified to require the officers to put on their jewels before entering the
Lodge and enter the Lodge Room in procession before the Opening Ritual of the
Lodge begins, as directed by the Grand Lecturer.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to eliminate the distribution o f the
Officers' Jewels at the opening of the Lodge and to adopt the procedure and
procession currently used in the Opening of Grand Lodge.

§26340. ADV AN CEMENT.
A Lodge shall advance an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to
a higher degree if he has given satisfactory evidence, by ~
examination in open Lodge, that he is entirely proficient and
well qualified in the degrees which he has already taken. To
demonstrate such proficiency. an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft shall only be required to recite from memory the obligation
of each degree. together with the signs and modes of recognition
of each degree. Any number of applicants may be examined at
a meeting, but not more than five shall be examined at any one
time with the questions being asked in rotation. Such
examination shall be held in front of the East between the altar
and the Master's station.
If for any reason there is an erroneous conferral of a degree or
degrees, the candidate retains the status reached but must wait
one year and present an application for a higher degree or
degrees.

including a provision for the automatic restoration of previously forfeited fees of
Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts who have failed to advance.
When one thinks of all the reasons for becoming a Mason, the lengthy
proficiency now required is not one of them . The Signs and Obligations are!
Furthermore, many other jurisdictions have adopted this practice and have
benefited from doing so.
The proposed revision to Section 26330 automatically restores the
candidate who has failed to present himself for advancement. This would be done
without notice or investigation by the Lodge.
Other than that the resolution is consistent with the purpose of Grand
Lodge.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that a new Section 6205 be added to the
California Masonic Code to read as follows:

responsibility for potential conflicts of interest if he is "out of the loop"? Multiple
experiences in society have indicated the problems that arise when appointees are
given free reign.

§6205. DISTRIBUTION.
The Committee on Distribution shall receive from the Grand
Secretary all matters of business presented to the Grand Lodce
for its consjderatjon and shall review and assicn such matters to
the appropriate committees for their study and subsequent report
to the Grand Lodee.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Any legislation or other business matter that is proposed to Grand Lodge
has implications, sometimes subtle, which are unique to particular aspects or
components of the Fraternity. When any particular committee has insights or
experiences regarding such a matter, it is appropriate to ask it to review the
proposal and provide a report to the Grand Lodge. For this reason, Grand Lodge
has developed a system whereby proper committees are assigned business matters
to discuss and report upon.
In recent years, the distribution of these matters has been the responsibility
of the Grand Master. The proponents of this resolution seek to change that
distribution system by having three other committee chairmen receive all proposals
directly from the Grand Secretary and then decide to which committee the matters
should be referred.
The proponents note that such a system was in place in past years, and that
this system was "most effective in maintaining the checks and balances necessary
to remove the slightest possibility of conflict of interest between the proposers of
business matters before the Grand Lodge and those reporting on the proposals."
By implication, the proponents are suggesting that the current system is less
effective. Unfortunately, the proponents have not provided any data to prove that
this is indeed the case. The three members proposed for this new committee, all
chairmen of committees, have only a limited sphere of responsibility and expertise,
and none of them has an overall perspective of Grand Lodge. How can three
individuals, each with their own special interest, be better able to avoid potential
conflicts of interest, than is the Grand Master?
The Grand Master is an elected official. and accountable to the Grand
Lodge for his actions. He is vested with the responsibility of overseeing all
activities of Masonry in California. In contradistinction, these committee chairmen
are appointees. The proposed legislation will, if enacted, create a system in which
the Grand Master may be bypassed. How can the Grand Master assume

Furthermore, the Grand Master prepares, for each Annual
Communication, a series of recommendations. If he is not aware of other pending
legislation for that meeting, he may inadvertently submit a similar proposal to one
that is already under consideration. This is not only personally embarrassing for
him, but it is an inefficient way to conduct our business.
The proposed resolution is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy
and practice.

Report of the Committee on Finance:
Your Finance Committee estimates that this additional committee, if added
to the Grand Lodge structure, would cost approximately $2,000 per year.

PARTY
RULES OF PROCEDURE FOR ANNUAL AND SPECIAL
COMMUNIC ATIONS
The following Rules of Procedure shall govern the deliberations
at each Annual and Special Communicat ion of the Grand Lodge.
All committee reports must be in the hands of the Grand
Secretary by the close of business on the first day of the Communication.
Legislation shall be heard at the sessions on the second and subseq uent
days of the Communication. Each chainnan of a committee to which
legislation has been referred should be present at all times during the
sessions at which legislation will be cons idered until all reports from his
committee have been given. If a committeema n is not present and
prepared to report when called for, the Grand Secretary shall read the
committee's report. If the Grand Secretary does not then have a copy of
the report to read, the vote will be taken without that report.
The Jurisprudence Committee shall report only once, unless there
is a special matter before the Grand Lodge which the committee and
presiding officer believe warrant indiv idual attention. The presiding
officer shall announce the vote required for passage of each item before
discussion begins.

Resolution 96-13
Adjusts Minimum Dues for Inflation

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the minimum Lodge dues from
S 12 to $48 because of inflation since 1949.

The proponents of this resolution seek to allow a lodge to purchase a life
membership for any Past Master. They justify this Lodge expenditure as being
appropriate because it is a "continuing tribute and honor to a Past Master for his
faithful service".

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:

Several issues need to be addressed in this proposal. First of all, it is
debatable whether any man who is retired from a position is entitled to
"continuing" tribute, especially of a financial nature.
Secondly, providing such an award to all Past Masters acts to shift the
financial responsibility of the Lodge to the remaining brethren. This latter group
will probably include members who were not even members of the Lodge when
that Past Master provided his service. rt is likely that some newer members could
resent having to accept the additional economic burden. Even though this
resentment were never mentioned by that member, it can act as a divisive force in
the Lodge.
Finally, one of the obligations of Masonry is a life-long commitment to
the support ofone's Lodge. The bestowing of a Lodge-endowed life membership
removes this commitment from the recipient. While it is currently possible to
provide that benefit to an out-going Master, it is contrary to the purposes of
Masonry, even under that circumstance.
This resolution is not consistent with our current policies and general
purposes.

WHEREAS, there is ample evidence that the cost-of-living has
skyrocketed during the Twentieth Century, as indicated by the cost of postage
st3mps (from 2 cents to 32 cents), housing, food, clothing, and other goods and
services;
WHEREAS, the minimum dues were raised twice during the first half of
this century from $6 to $9 in 1918 and from $9 to $12 in 1949, on each occasion
to the amount of the average dues at that time;
WHEREAS, the current minimum dues of$12 were adopted by the Grand
Lodge in 1949, and no adjustment has been made for inflation since that time;
WHEREAS, inflation in the first half of this century was very low (a
factor of two) and, in the last fifty years, a ten-fold increase in inflation has been
experienced, indicating that the current minimum dues should be in the vic inity of
$120;
WHEREAS, by ignoring the effects of inflation for the last half century,
Freemasonry has allowed itself to fall far behind societal standards for membership
in fraternal organizations;
WHEREAS, a study entitled Why Are We Selfing Masonry So Cheap 7 , by
K.G. Sample and K.B. Sample, Greenville Lodge No. 10, Greenville, MO shows
that our good brethren who founded the Lodges in this country since 1850
committed a far greater percentage of their income to the growth of Freemasonry
than our present brethren do, as indicated in the following table of wages, dues and
hours worked to pay their dues, extracted from their report:

The minimum annual dues are $12. throu~ December 31. 1996.
Effective Januarv I. 1997. the minimum annual dues are $48.

following the conferring of the Master Mason Degree or as

WHEREAS, these brethren (our predecessors) were responsible for the
building of many magnificent Lodges which were the main attractions in towns
throughout this country;
WHEREAS, people tend to place a value on goods and services in
proportion to their cost;
WHEREAS, surveys have revealed that many prospective younger
applicants for membership are surprised at the low membership dues in Lodges,
and there is some indication that an increase in dues to a more appropriate level
may actually encourage applications for membership by younger men;
WHEREAS, in the present competitive world, Freemasonry must compete
with other organizations for the attention and retention of younger members;
WHEREAS, at the 1995 Annual Communication, the brethren of this
jurisdiction rejected a Resolution seeking a one-step adjustment of the minimum
dues from $12 to $80, far less than the amount of$120 which would be consistent
with inflation;
WHEREAS, many brethren expressed the opinion that a gradual increase
in dues would be more acceptable than a single large increase;
WHEREAS, the increased minimum dues in 1918 and 1949 reflected the
average dues in those times;
WHEREAS, the average dues in this Jurisdiction are currently almost $42,
only slightly more than three times the minimum dues established in J949·
)

WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California will celebrate its 150th
Anniversary in the year 2000 and, as it enters the Twenty-first Century, it would
be appropriate to do so with a dues structure which is more consistent with the
economy of the period;
WHEREAS, a goal of $100 minimum dues by January I, 2000 is
reasonable and consistent with the economy; and
WHEREAS, the first step in adjusting the minimum dues to $48 (slightly
above the current average) is not expected to cause a hardship on Lodges or
members and, in fact, will have no effect on Lodges whose dues are now well
above the average.

§27020. LIFE MEMBERSHIP.
A Lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a system
of life membership, which shall forever exempt a member from
the payment of dues therein. The resolution or any amendment
shall not be acted on at the Stated Meeting at which it is
introduced, or until notice in writing has been forwarded by mail
to every member of the Lodge. It must provide that life
membership shall be granted upon payment of a sum of money
named therein, which sum shall in case the annual dues are SH
ill be not Jess than ~ aQQ.Q and the minimum amount be
proportionately greater as the dues are greater; or, in the
altemati<1e, it may provide for the granting of such a life
membership upon payment of a sum of money equal to the
annual dues of the Lodge multiplied by the factor indicated
opposite the member's age in the following schedule:
Under age 49, 2 1 times annual dues;
50 to 54 inclusive, 19 times annual dues;
55 to 59 inclusive, 17 times annual dues;
60 to 64 inclusive, 14 times annual dues;
65 and over, 11 times annual dues;
shall then become an executed contract requiring the consent of
the Lodge and the life member to rescind it. The resolution shall
take effect only upon its approval by the Grand Master.
When the annual dues of the Lodge are increased, the Lodge's
standing life membership resolution shall be deemed to have
been amended without further action of the Lodge to increase the

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. ofCalifornia:

of services for the Grand Lodge of California, and its constituent boards and
committe es;
WHEREAS, the traditional assistant to the Grand Secretary has been the
appointed office of Assistant Grand Secretary;
WHEREAS, the position of Assistant Grand Secretary was discontin ued
by vote of Grand Lodge in I 994, along with the position of Assistant Grand
Treasurer;
WHEREA S, the experienc e of the Grand Secretary's Office without an
Assistant Grand Secretary has been less than satisfactory; and
WHEREAS, it is desirable in the opinion of the Grand Secretary to restore
the position of Assistant Grand Secretary as an appointed officer of Grand Lodge.

and 5020 of the Californi a Masonic Code be amended as marked:

All of this costs money. Ten years ago, the Masonic Homes expenses
were $12.3 million for the year. This past year, our expenses amounted to $23.9
million. For many years, a part of the operating funds were derived from a per
capita charge of from $1 .00 to $2.00 per member per year. In l 981, the $1 .00
assessment was discontinued and we have since been dependent on voluntary
contributions, which is exemplary on the part of Masons.
We all receive many appeals each year to support charitable causes. Many
Masons have made the Masonic Homes their favorite charity for many reasons.
Their voluntary gifts along with prudent investments of the funds, yields income
to provide for the operation and maintenance of the Homes, of which we can all be
proud. We deeply appreciate the generous financial support given by the Masons
and widows of this jurisdiction.
The trustees of the Masonic Homes wish to thank our Grand Master, the
Most Worshipful Charles H. Alexander, for his support and attendance at several
events at the Homes during the year.
In closing, 1 would like to read a letter which is a sample of the
expressions we receive from relatives of residents at the Homes.
Admissio ns Committ ee
by Viclor Howard, Ph.D., and Ernest A. Pooleon, Co-Chair men
Prior to the full Board Meeting, on the first Wednesday of each month, the
eight Trustees who fonn the Admissions Committee, four from the North and four
from the South, have received and carefully studied the applications for Masonic
assistance. These Trustees evaluate the applications and submit their comment s
and votes to the two co-chainnen. The co-chairmen then discuss the results of the
vote by phone, and where significant difference s occur, meetings are arranged to
take place prior to the regular Board Meeting, at which time Homes Staff and
Administrators attend and assist in the discussion.
Over the past several years experience has indicated that an overnight visit
to one of the facilities by all applicants is essential in order that Administrators and
Medical Staff can evaluate them and assist in determining the most appropriate
placement. (The facility visited is not an indication of where the most appropria te

In addition to planning and providing activities and events for the Homes'
centennial, the committee is planning the events and program for the annual
conference of the Masonic Homes Executives' Association of North America that
will be hosted by the Masonic Homes of California, June 19 - 24, 1998. To date,
arrangements for hotel meeting space and guest rooms have been made, some
potential topics and speakers have been identified, and a financial agreement to
cover some conference costs has been made with the Association. Logistical
requirements and a budget for the conference are being developed.
Financial Planning and Budget Committee

by Stanley M Cazneaux. PGM. Chairman
The Financial Planning and Budget Committee of the Masonic Homes of
California, Board of Trustees, presently includes the Chainnan and two members,
Right Worshipful Allen B. Gresham and Worshipful Frederick L. Sorsabal. The
committee's work could not be completed without the excellent advice and counsel
of our Chief Financial Officer, Douglas A. Scott. The committee would like to
express its sincere appreciation to Brother Scott for his help and support.
The Financial Planning and Budget Committee acknowledges with
appreciation the continued support, guidance and counsel provided by Most
Worshipful Roy J. Henville, President of the Masonic Homes of California, and
Very Worshipful Thomas C. Holm, Grand Treasurer.

Insurance Committee

by Richard 0. Wright. Chairman
Earthquake insurance, and the lack of it, continues to be the number one
insurance problem for our Masonic Homes. Even though we were able to secure
a small additional layer of coverage this year, the costs continue to climb.
The Board of Trustees is convinced the long term solution is not with the
traditional insurance marketplace but rather with our "self-insured" fund. An
additional contribution of approximately $300,000 will be added for the 199611997
fiscal year bringing our two year total to approximately $1, I 00,000. It is estimated
that similar contributions will be needed for the next 8 - I 0 years before the fund
will be significantly large enough to replace the limit of coverage that we now
purchase.

Personnel Committee

Long Range Planning Committee

by Fred Sorsabal, Chairman
A new committee for Long Range Planning was appointed by Roy
Henville,PGM, President of the Masonic Homes Board, to provide a document that
would enable the Board of Trustees and members of our Fraternity to provide
quality care for eligible elders and children in the 21st Century.
The committee has been working diligently to determine what type of care
should be given in the future, particularly with the tremendous changes in geriatric
care and to make sure that our Masonic Homes continue to provide the quality care
that is expected at our Homes at Union City and Covina. A survey was sent out to
all Masonic Homes in the United States to see where they are headed in relation to
the surrender of assets and the pay for service question. The committee recognizes
that a change in the admission's policy would, by necessity, be brought before
Grand Lodge, and it was determined that further exploration of this question must
continue.
With significant changes in care for the elderly, the committee feels that
for the next five (5) years the population at Covina and Union City will remain
approximately the same as now. It has been determined that the Admissions
Requirements should remain as they now are - that is, a person must be ambulatory
and independent to seek admission. It is of concern to the committee the growing
number of our residents who need Assisted Care or Skilled Nursing Facilities in the
short time after admission to either facility. so the committee will be studying the
future needs for additional facilities for this type of care. Changes have already
been approved at Covina for this increased care. It has also been determined that
in the foreseeable future, no SNF should be built at Covina.

Physical Facilities

by William Dickson, Chairman
Union City
This past year has been both exciting and difficult. We have been
engaged in a major remodeling of the Wollenberg building. The interior was taken
down to the structural elements and rebuilt to change its use from a Skilled Nursing
Faci lity to a combination ofliving units on the upper floors and a Health Cente r on
the lower floor.

In addition, we have added a second generator room for emergency power
to the entire site, and garden areas so that residents who were previously somewhat
limited in access to these parts of life, will be able to enjoy outdoor experiences.
Complications occured when a difficult relationship developed with our
architects and it was felt it was in the best interest of the Home to terminate our
contract. Replacement architects have been employed and the progress pace
resumed although there were still bumps due to hidden underground obstructions
and material delays. The net result of all this is a several months delayed opening.
Overall though it is exciting to see this new dimension deve lop for our
residents. We have kept them up-to-date with the construction progress by means
ofa "Sidewalk Superintendent's Report", which were video films made in-house
and broadcast over our Channel 3.
Simultaneous with th is we have completed the remodel plans for the
Ad ams building. These are currently out for b ids by subcontractors. The
assistance of consultant and contractor services should be noted. Henry Coil of
Tilden-Coil Constructors along with his Vice President, Dean Irving, have been an
immense help. Henry is a member of Riverside and Evergreen Lodges. His fathe r
is the author ofCoil's Encyclopedia which is denoted to Masonry. Dean has been
with the committee countless hours at no expense to the Homes, providing
valueable engineering and suggestions. Subsequently we ne gotiated a contract with
them to construct on an "open book" basis and a very low % of profit. Lou
Gehwicks of Gerontological Planning Associates is a recog nized authority in the
field of geronto logy and architectural planning for the elderly. He has been a
valuable consultant from the beginning survey of need, schematic layouts of
concepts and helping clarify relocation of residents as we work through the
remain ing building with residential apanments. He has challenged our thinking
and he has taken a particular interest in our facilities as a unique and successful
aproach to care for the elderly. Coming from a professional whose life has been
devoted to planning for the elderly on a two continent basis, it is a tribute to all the
leaders, Trustees, and brethren of this jurisdiction the last I 00 years.
