Report of the Administrator
Masonic Homes, Covina
1995-1996

Assisted Living facility, much to the delight of our in-house residents as well as the
seven residents who had been out-placed. It was a day I was especially proud of,
and a day which was fulfilling for all of our staff who had made this new service
possible.

This past year was another transitional year at the Masonic Home at
Covina, and it is with a sense of pride that I report to you the progress our
employees made in implementing new programs to better serve the children and
seni~r ~itizens of our community. At a~proximately this same time last year,
Covm.a s ~anagement tea~ gathered to discuss where we were as a care-giving
org.anizat10n and what might be done to address the changing needs of our
residents. Although many reparatory steps had been taken in our immediate past
~o address our resident's changing needs, all of us agreed we had reached a point
m o~r development where comprehensive changes were necessary if we were to
provide for the contemporary needs of our clientele. And as has been typical of our
e~ployees' performance in the past, they proved equal to the challenge of our new
circumstances by proposing and eventually implementing five major programs to
improve our care-giving efforts at Covina.
Perhaps the most rewarding work undertaken by our staff during the past
year was the establishment of Assisted Living accommodations within our Senior
Care complex. Upon examining the needs of our aging Senior residents, it was
clear to ~ur Adult H~alt.h Care staff that establishment of an Assisted Living
~ommumty was essential if we were to provide our residents the opportunity to age
m place for the maximum period of time.
Assist~d Living ~are is an intermediate level of care between Independent
. .
L1vtng and Skilled Nursmg care. Its purpose is to provide care for those with
mod~rate to heavy levels of fraility who need daily personal assistance, but do not
require the health care services administered within a skilled nursing environment.
Although an. element of this level of care was being provided under contract with
the ~isiting Nur.sing Association (VNA}, we were not positioned to provide the
qualtty or quantity of care which inevitably would be required as a result of the
aging of our Independent Living residents. In fact, at the time of our decision to
es~~l~sh an ~ssisted Living service, seven of our residents had been out-placed at
fac1ht1es which were better structured to provide the level of care we were about
to establish.

In order to provide Assisted Living care within a reasonable period of time
while maintaining costs at the lowest possible level, we decided to convert our
Ash:-Vood b~i.lding, ~r~viously. an Independent Living building, into a full-fledged
Assisted L1vmg fac1hty. Thts undertaking took approximately four months to
complete, including all necessary building renovations and the hiring of additional
nursing staff. And on February 29, 1996 we proudly opened the doors to our new

Our child care staff was no less aggressive in identifying and
implementing programs designed to better meet the needs of our typical child
resident. Unlike the children who were residents at the Home twenty to twenty-five
years ago, the typical child today comes to us from circumstances which might ~st
be described as psychologically traumatizing. As a result, our model of care which
was so successful with previous generations was not the model to best serve current
residents.
After extensive review of each child's needs and after reviewing the
multitude of child care programs in place at facilities similar to ours, our
management staff recommended we pursue a relationship with .Boys Tow~ for the
purpose of retraining our houseparents in contemporary .techniques of ch.1ld care.
Our Board of Trustees enthusiastically endorsed this recommendation and
beginning May l, 1996 we engaged the services of Boys Town to train our child
care staff. As of this report, all training has been completed and the Boys Town
model of child care is in active placement here at the Home.
Our new model of child care include such hallmarks as: a) direct care staff
autonomy (decentralization); b) skill-based training; c) data-based approach;~)
systematic procedl!res; e) consumer orientation (chil.d input); and, t) ~ emphasis
on regular staff evaluations. This approach provides our staff with concrete
practices and procedures for implementing individualized youth trea~e.nt plans
while facilitating youth progress toward treatment goals. In add1t10n, the
establishment of a specific model of care provides such advantages~ red~ced staff
ambiguity relative to the children's and management's expectatt~ns, mcreased
consistency during staff turnover thus stabilizing youth behaviors, and the
opportunity for improved data collection to support staff efforts.
Jf our first three months after implementation are any indication of what
we can expect from our new program in the l?ng run'. there is little doubt we ha.ve
embarked upon a course from which our children will greatly benefit. Behavior
among the general population has improved dramatic~lly, and school perfonnance
as measured by grades earned during the summer session has mar~edly chang~d for
the better. Our ultimate goal is to prepare our children to meet with suc~ess m ~he
world outside the Masonic Home, and we believe this new program w~ll provide
our children with the skills and sense of responsibility necessary to do JUSt that.
In addition to our new model of child care, we also implemented three
other programs which are designed to improve our childre n's chances _for success
during and after their residency at the Home. The first of these is our new

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mentoring program which employs the talents and experiences of previous
generations of Masonic Home's children. Specifically, we invited alumnae of the
Home, no matter what their age, to serve as a big brother or big sister to a current
child resident. The thought behind this program was that our alumnae could
identify with the challenges confronting our children, and based upon their own
experiences, help our children work through the difficulties of living in a Group
Home. To date, seven of our alumnae are participatin g in this new program, and
our children have enthusiastically welcomed their participation.
We have also implemented a new tutoring program to help our children
improve their academic performance. In addition to improved staffing, the program
has been revised to require our children to attend regular tutoring sessions in our
library, each and every night, until such time as they improve their academic
standing. We have found this structured approach to be a powerful incentive for
our children to improve their academic performanc e.
Finally, in this past year we introduced a new program for our graduating
children which is designed to provide them with the maximum opportunity to
succeed in their post-high school studies or early career work. This new program
is entitled our TLC program, or, our "Transitional Level of Care" program .
After researching the lives of recent alumnae of the Home, it became
evident many of the children who had left the Home immediately upon graduation ,
were not meeting with the success we had hoped for. Reasons for this lack of
success were varied; however, there was one element common to many. Our
children lacked the emotional support often required during the latter stages of
adolescence.

alike were provided with an abundance of happy experiences throughout the year
as well. None of us will ever forget the excitement on the faces of our children as
they prepared to participate in this year's Rose Parade in costumes made by our
Senior residents. And those of us who accompanied our children on their
educational trip to Washington D .C. and New York City will never forget the looks
of awe on the children's faces as they visited many of our nation's awe-inspiring
sights.
It was indeed a memorable year, and all of us at the Home will always
remember that without the benevolence of the members of the Masonic Fraternity,
none of this would be possible. Once again, on behalfofth e staff and residents of
the Masonic Home at Covina, I thank you for your support, and pledge to you that
the staff at Covina will continue to work relentlessly to improve our service to
those we lovingly call our Masonic family.

.
In order to provide our graduates with improved emotional support, we
implement ed three transitional care programs which, if elected by the graduate,
permitted him or her to remain at the Home while preparing for adult life.
Requirements to remain in good standing in this program are satisfactory progress
toward earning a post-high school degree/certificate, or satisfactory performance
in an entry level job. In addition, each graduate (now known officially as a
"guest") must be an outstanding example of good behavior for our resident
children, and volunteer a specified number of hours each week in service to the
Home, preferably helping our children with their academic studies. To date, two
Homes' graduates have chosen to participate in the TLC program, and both are
succeeding in their efforts to earn their college degrees. Given the success of this
program, we will encourage more of our graduates to take advantage of this
improved opportunity for success.
Although this past year was a transition year filled with many hours of
intensive work, it was also a gratifying year for all of us who work here at the
Home. Not only did we implement many positive changes, but staff and residents

REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWME NT BOARD

361

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand
Lodge, Brethren; I am pleased to present to you a summary report of the activities
of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board for the year 199S-1996.
Total contributions from the brethren of the Grand Lodge for the fiscal
year beginning July I, 1995 and ending June 30, 1996, including contributions
through United Way, amounted to $1,l 12,S95.81. This number represents a
decrease of$134,316.76 from last year's total of$1 ,246,912.S7. Over the past ten
years, the addition to the Endowment Fund from membership contributions has
ranged from a high of approximatel y $1,490,000 down to this year's figure of
$I, 112,596. This represents a decrease of about 2S%. It does not give us a very
comfortable feeling in considering the future of our Masonic Homes.
The average gift received per contributor was $2S.30, as compared to
$26.74 last year. Jn addition, the average donation per member throughout the
Grand Lodge was $10.11, a decrease of about six percent under the $10.70 average
last year.
Of the 437 lodges in the Grand Lodge, I SS (or 3S%) achieved the Honor
Roll with an average gift of$10.70. Unfortunately, this is, again, fewer lodges and
a smaller percentag7 than the previous year.
Other gifts to the Endowment Fund were as follows:
Bequests ... .. . ....... . . .. ... ... $3,665, 108.44
General Undesignated .......... . ..... . 1,750.15
Memorials ....... .. .. ... . .... ..... .. 5,449.90
Royalties . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 143.52
The Grand Total is .... ... ..... ... $4,785,047.6 2
These numbers show how important the bequests are to the growth of our
Endowment Fund. They serve as a strong reminder th at, when a brother
remembers the Masonic Homes in his will, he leaves a bright and lasting memorial
of his personal dedication to the principles of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
As we all know, over the past years we have wimessed a continual decline
in membership, effecting the amount of money added to the permanent endowment
fund . In addition to the membership decline, however, we have also witnessed a
decline in the percentage of the brethren who make a contribution. In the 1985-87
period over 50% of the brethren made contributions. For the past two years only

40% have done so. It appears that our lodges are simply not giving adequate
attention to this major charity. We certainly hope to see an improvement in the
future.

Most Worshipful, on behalf of the 35 members of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, I thank you for the opportunity of serving you and the Grand

I want to hasten to add a sincere note of appreciation to those hardworking lodge secretaries and Lodge Endowment Fund Chairmen who do so much
to help this program. Without their dedication, we could not be nearly as
successful as we are. They are asked to submit contributions on a timely basis,
report numbers of contributors, and include the name of any brother giving over
$50. This infonnation is critical to monitoring the progress of the Endowment
Board program. To those who do that job I say "Thank you!" I encourage every
Master to ensure that he has a designated Endowment Fund Chainnan. Having a
brother assigned to this responsibility is a major step toward a successful fund drive
in your lodge.
The members of your Endowment Board continue to present the Masonic
Homes history book entitled, "The Greatest of These is Charity" to newly-initiated
Entered Apprentice Masons, whenever we are advised that a degree is to be
conferred. We also are anxious to give talks and reports, make slide presentations,
and in as many ways as possible support the lodges in their Masonic Homes
programs.
Three of our members found it necessary to resign from the Board at the
end of this year; Milburn Cobb, Willie Mock, and Lloyd Nickerson. We sincerely
appreciate their service over the past years. Several new members joined the Board
this year; Allen Palmer, Don Lindenau, Tom Magee, Donald Franke, Billie Bowles,
Jim Ward, Ken Nagel, and Galen Niedenfuehr. Bruce Johansen rejoined the Board
after a year of work in another state.
May I close with another reminder that the income from the Endowment
Fund accounts for a significant amount of the resources needed to keep our Homes
in operation. With the combination of continued inflation and declining
membership, it is more critical than ever that every brother do his part in building
the Endowment Fund. I encourage every Master, Warden, Secretary and Lodge
Masonic Homes Chairman to re-dedicate himself to communicati ng this message
to the brethren of his lodge. We must not disappoint our brethren, sweethearts and
children who live in the Homes. They are counting on us.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California :
Brethren :
As you know, the recognition process is complete. Lodges all over the
g relationships with our Prince Hall Brethren. The final part of
developin
are
state
this process took place in January when the Grand Lodge of Hawaii, under the
leadership of Grand Master Benny Ing, passed legislation recognizing the Most
Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge ofCalifor ia and Hawaii, Inc. Then in July
a similar piece of legislaiton came to Hawaii from the Prince Hall Grand Lodge,
under the leadership of M :. w... Joseph V. Nicholas.
It seems like it was just a short time ago that Resolution 91-7 started this
long journey. A journey that has been a labor of love for all that were involved.
Committe es from both Grand Lodges worked long and hard to bring mutual
recognition to fruition . The wisdom of M:. W :. Ted Meriam, the organizational
talents of our former chairman , Paul Hodiak, the much needed input from Carlos
Castenad a, Ed Long, Jim Vaughn and Doug Young. Each and every member of

370

the team made contributions throughout the process. We also need to thank our
Junior Grand Warden, Mel Nahin, for his help and guidance during the final phases
of this process. It's not very often yu can get "free" legal advice~ We also want
to thank our Prince Hall counterparts for their patience and understanding for
without it we wouldn't have gotten to first base. Many splendid friendships were
spawned from this joint committee.
Our two Grand Lodges made history this last July when, for the first time,
our two Grand Masters met together at the tiled 141" Annual Grand Sessions of the
Prince Hall Grand Lodge. Your whole executive committee, M .. W:. Alexander,
R:.W:. Gresham, R:.W-. Wordlow and R:.W:. Nahin were in attendance. Many
of the Grand Lodge Officers were also in attendance as well as your truly. Also in
attendance were the Prince Hall Grand Masters of Arkansas, Georgia and New
Mexico. This was a first for them as well.

Now today we are making history in our Grand Lodge. This is the first
time these two Grand Lodges have met in tiled session at our Annual
Communication. I'm sure M :. W:. Joseph V. Nicholas wil have something to say
about it later. In the event you haven't heard about my connection to M :. W :.
Nicholas, he and I were stationed at Oxnard Air Force Base together in 1962, 1963
and 1964. He and a friend of his taught me how to play pool, more specifically,
nine ball. Sure I lost a few nickels but it was worth it. Little did we know what the
future would hold for us.
Jn closing, I would like to thank M :.W:. Ron Sherod for the vision he had
for this committee and for allowing me to be a part of it. It truly has been a labor
of love. And now thank you " Brethren". You passed the legislation to make
recognition possible and now you have the responsibility of building upon the
relationships you have already started with our Prince Hall Brethren.
Thank you, Most Worshipful.
Respectfully submitted,
Francis A. Russell, Jr. Chairman

Executiv e Secretari es

Blood Banks

The roster of Executive Secretaries remains unchange d from last year.
These men who endeavor to serve Freemaso nry locally as well as globally should
be and are appreciat ed by the members of the committe e.

Five of the Service Bureaus provide and maintain a Blood Bank. The
Bureaus that provide this service to our Fraternity are Sacramen to, San Francisco,
Bakersfield, East Bay and Central Valley (Fresno). It should be noted that some
of the regional Blood Banks are changing their methods of tracking credits for
individua l groups such as ours. Vrej Mekhalian, Executive Secretary of the San
Francisco Bureau, is involved with such a change. The final impact of these
changes has yet to be determine d.

Committ ee Meetings
. This year_ the committe e held two informati onal meetings for the
Executive Secretane s. The first meeting was held in Pasadena at the Pasadena
~cottish Rite Center o~ Sa~day, March 23, 1996. The purpose of the meeting, as
m years past, was d1stnbut1on and explanation of the several report forms required
to put together the annual statistical analysis. This year's analysis is detailed at the
end of this narrative. At the same meeting, Bro. Jack Doughty of the Orange
C?unty Bureau told the story of a Brother Mason who had passed away in Texas.
His ~elat_ives, wanting this Brother to be buried in Californi a, transporte d the
remam~ m the _rear seat of their Cadillac, only to be stopped at the Agricultural
Ins~ct1on Station at the California-Nevada Border. The Orange County Masonic
Se~1ce Bureau was brought in to assist in completing the odyssey, and the bizarre
episode was covered in the local media. The second meeting was held in the Grand
Lodge Office_ con~erence room on Friday, April 12, 1996. It, like the meeting in
Southern Cahforn1a, was for dissemina tion of the report forms and discussio n of
problems the bureaus had encounter ed. Bro. Amie Asercion informed the
commi_ttee th~t due to his declining health, he was resigning from the East Bay
Masonic Service Bureau. The committee, at the request of the Fresno Bureau and
due to the diligent work of their Executive Secretary , Warren Carr, changed the
name to the Central Valley Masonic Service Bureau.

Lodges and the local Service Bureau, were finalized for the following Lodges :

Operatin g Expenses

A quick review of the Recapitulation of Service Bureau Operating
Expenses reveals the care taken by the Executive Secretaries in keeping close to or
well within the Bureau Budget. This year $10,597.80 more was expended by the
several Bureaus compared to the prior fiscal year.

Conclusi on
Bush Masonic Relief Inc.
Bush Masonic Relief Inc. is the primary source of funding for Los
~ngeles, Long Beach and San Gabriel Valley Bureaus, the three Service Bureaus
m the greater Los Angeles area. This fund, which provides a majority of the funds
for these Bureaus, is the result of very careful investmen t by the trustees of the
fund. This committee wishes to acknowledge the heard work of the Trustees, Wor.
Bro. Ralph Head, Wor. Bro. A. _Bruce Ivie, and Right Worshipf ul Bro. Mel Nahin,
who currently serves as our Junior Grand Warden. Special recognitio n is given to
Wor. Bro. Ralph Head. Wor. Bro. Head has resigned as a Trustee, and his position

The past year was a quiet one as far as any major changes in the overall
operation of this committe e. The coming year will bring changes in the Greater
San Francisco Bay Area as there will be a consolidation of the San Francisco , East
Bay and Southern Alameda Bureaus. The issue of changes in Blood Bank
reporting and group credits hopefully will be resolved soon.
This committe e was successful in publishin g the updated Rules and
Regulations as they appertain to Masonic Service Bureaus.
This committee sincerely appreciate s the support it has received from the
Most Worshipful Charles H. Alexander, the elected and appointed corps of officers,

On beha lf of the mem bers of your Mem
orial Service Committee,

We have come to the place of recognition of
those who have preceded us
and have completed their ques t for the ultim
ate light whic h shines in the lives of
all men everywhere but particularly within those
who recognize the great I AM as
the Creator and Lord of us all.
We, as Master Masons, come to do homage to
the memory of our departed
brethren who have arrived at the place wher
e dwells that house not made with
hands eternal in the heavens. We can never do
justice in recognition to their work
and service that has been completed , nor can we
be thankful enough to them for the
paths that they have blazed upon the ashes of
those of our brethren who have gone
before them or for the building of the frater
nity which they have assisted in
erecting.
Thei r work is.completed. The trowel is set
aside and they have now
entered into a much deserved rest from their labor
s but their works do follow them
and for this, we too, give our prayer of gratit
ude and thanks. The silver cord is
loosed, the golden bowl is broken, the pitcher
is broken at the fountain and the well
is broken at the cistern. The dust has returned
to the earth as it was and the spirit
has returned to God who gave it.
Although we miss them sadly, we rejoice in
the thought that they have
traveled to that bourne of time and space from
which no traveler returns and are at
long last home ; our eternal home, prepared
from eternity, for all of those who
profess their faith in God and pledge their alleg
iance to Him at the great altar of
life, with heart, head and hand s upon the Holy
Bible of the Almighty Architect of
the Universe.

This year we have recorded the passing of 3,829 of our brethren. They
have included so very many of our friends and loved ones. Some highly
distinguished within our fraternity and some not so well recognized but now, ALL,
on equal tenns and equal recognition before God's throne of Grace.
This past year say the passing of our Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems,
and here to bring us his memorial remembrance is one who knew and loved him
best, our Past Grand Master of 1993-1994, the Most Worshipful Warren J.
Blom seth .
We wish to also acknowledge the passing of Worshipful Brother Emmen
Shaw, Assistant Grand Organist, and here to share his memorial tribute is our
Grand Secretary, the Very Worshipful John L. Cooper 111.
For those of us who be live in the Immortality of the soul and Eternity, we
can say with the poet of old:
As sweetly as a child whom neither
Thought disturbs, nor care encumbers:
Tired with the long play, at close of summer's day,
Lies down and slumbers.
He set as sets the morning star which goes
Not down behind the darkened west, or hides
Obscured among the tempests of the sky,
But melts away into the light of heaven.
Oh, let us trust, with holy men of old,
Not all the story here begun is told.
So the tired spirit, waiting to be freed,
On life's last leaf, with tranquil eye shall read,
By the pale glimmer of the torch reversed,
Not finis, but the end of volume first.
LIFE'S RACE WELL RUN,
LIFE'S WORK WELL DONE,
LIFE'S CROWN WELL WON.
NOW COMES REST!
Brethren, if you please rise. and remain standing in reverence to the
memory of these our departed brethren as we pray and end our tribute today with
the playing of"TapsK.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M o/California:
The Charter for the Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools is found
in Section 6060 of the California Masonic Code and reads as follows: "The
Committee on Public Schools shall develop and promote methods of increasing
interest in and support for the Public Schools." The activities and achievements
outlined in the following report are founded on these 20 words.

Grand Master's Proclamation
For the seventy-sixth annual Pub lic Schools Week (now Mont h)
observance our Grand Master, Charles H. Alexander, adopted the theme of his
Proclamation a quotatU>n from the early 20th century writer, Henry Brook Adam:
•A Teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops."
In his proclamation he reminded us that the schools of this state have
never before faced such challenges as they have over the last several decades, with
literally dozens of different languages and dialects in the classroom; a society that
has grown increasingly violent and which tends to reject many of .the values
associated with education; a society with an increasing percentage of children from
single parent families and homes with declining parental interest in education.
Grand Master Alexander has urged us to redouble our efforts to aid and
support our public schools, to give strong support to the Masonic Student
Assistance Program to help deal with the problems of drug and alcohol abus~ and
to support those dedicated teachers who are the vanguards of the educational
struggle that our society faces today .
This year, as in all previous years, the constituent lodges of Califo~ia
have been urged to obtain such proclamations from l~al city.and ~ounty officials.
Notably, we have obtained proclamations from P.res1dent ~111 Chnto.n, Gove_rnor
Pete Wilson from the State Superintendent of Public Instruction, Delaine Eastin as
well as from some of the larger school districts of California. These are all

386

387

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LOIXJE OF C AUFORNIA

appreciated and help to serve our purpose of publicizing and promoting the cause
of our Public Schools of California.

The five teachers so honored are as follows: Mr. Cedric Anderson of
Bellflower; Mrs. Sandra Fleishman of Agoura; Mrs. Emma Glover of Hanford; Mr.
John McQuire of Arcata; and Mr. Javier Gonzalez of Whittier.

Public Schools Month
By far the most important event of the school year is the annual
observance of what heretofore has been termed Public Schools Week, but which
?rand '."faster Al~x~der_ has changed to Public Schools Month. This takes place
m April. Ou~ ob1ect1ve is to increase the public's awareness of and appreciation
for our public schools. To promote this event all Public Schools Committee
members were assigned to Lodges in their areas with instructions to contact them
at their district officers association meetings and to generate enthusiasm and
support for ~is endeavo~. The committeemen meet with the incoming Senior
Wardens and increase their awareness that this is one of the truly important events
of the Masonic year, give ideas and instruction on what materials are available
through the Grand Lodge Supply Office and how best to use them as promotional
materials.

Masons on Campus
During the year 1996 the Los Angeles Unified School District Board of
Education has continued to cooperate with the local Masons in the implementation
of the Masons on Campus Program. Volunteers have worked successfully with
students and staff as classroom aids, as school volunteers, as community resource
persons, as aids to the handicapped and as volunteers with special skills. The
program has been under the direction of Brother Donald Pollock. Its success in the
Los Angeles area points up the need for its continuance and expansion to other
areas of the State.
Teacher of the Year Awards
. . For several years the Public Schools Committee has helped to support and
subs1d1ze the Outstanding Teacher of the Year Program. On January 12'\ the
Grand Lodge again participated in the honoring of five outstanding California
Teachers of the Year. Most Worshipful Charles H. Alexander represented the
Grand Lodge and the Masons of California and presented each of the five winning
teachers a beautiful certificate and a cash award of $1,000 for the purchase of
~lassroom material, class programs or the purchase of educational items for the
improvement of their schools.
The presentation was moderated by State Superintendent of Public
fnstruct_ion, ?elaine Eastin, at the end of the January 12, 1996 monthly meeting of
the California State Board of Education. The event was open to the public.

Masonic Model Student Assistance Program
The Grand Lodge Public Schools Committee, working closely with the
California Masonic Foundation, assists in publicizing and implementing the MSAP
program. The Public Schools Chairman and other representatives attend the
Foundation meetings and offer input where appropriate. Likewise, the Chairman
of the Foundation and other interested members of the Foundation are invited to
attend the Public Schools Committee meetings. This procedure has proven to be
a highly effective path of communication between the two committees.
Committee Meetings
Two meetings were convened by our committee during the year 19951996. The first was held at the Hawthorne Masonic Center in Southern California
on March 10th, the second at Grand Lodge on October 15th. These meetings are
generally quite productive and tend to generate a spirit of esprit d' corps among the
members of the committee, generating a sense of direction and a feeling of
common purpose and endeavor.
School Boxes
The school box program which for the past two years was promoted and
carried forth throughout the State with generally mixed reviews was phased out this
year. Practically all of these boxes were used by lodges to augment their Public
Schools Month program. There is at this time no plan for reordering and renewing
the program. It was successful in many places where it was used effectively, but
many lodges were unable or unwilling to implement it in their areas.
Little Red School House Pins
The little red school house pins have been a very popular item for the past
several years. They are given to teachers and school personnel and often time~ to
the public who attend school open houses during Public Schools Month. In view
of their popularity we continue to urge lodges to purchase them in quantities at
$1 .25 each for distribution at these events and other Masonic gatherings.

Support in the Senate
For years, Senator Ralph Dills has been a valued member of the Grand
Lodge Public Schools Committee and a staunch supporter of the Public Schools of
California . We regret that due to the frailty of his health and that of his family plus
the added responsibility of having been recently appointed to the task of being a
Senate Committe e Chairman , he must resign from this committee. However, he
assures us that he will continue to strive for the public support and improvem ent
of the public schools of California. We thank him for all he has done for us in
keeping us informed of pending bills and legislation. We will miss him. We will
be depending to even a greater extent than ever on Brother Ray Young to keep us
up to date through the valuable newsletter which he promulgates several times each
year for our enlightenment.

after our flo~t was shown as the only Parade clip used in the headline introduction
to the _evenmg news. Further publicity was gained by an article written by the
Asso~1ated Press which mentione d Humpty Dumpty as one of the four crowdpleasmg floats m_ the Parade. We acknowledge that the advice of the float builder
to..enter a ~oat with popular appeal would get us more recognition than a float with
a Masonic message".

Riding on the 1997 float will be Grand Worthy Advisors from California,
Oklahom a, Michigan, Massachusetts, Florida, Washington/Idaho and Canada.
They will be dressed in fonnal gowns in the colors of the rainbow and will fonn
a Jiving rainbow around the large floral rainbow extending the entire length of the
float. In the center of the float, there will be a young lady who is an Amaranth
scholarsh ip recipient dressed in academic cap and gown depicting graduation as
one of life ' s shining moments .
The Committee has arranged for some special effects on the float to attract
the public attention, including stonn clouds at the rear with thunder and lightning
and simulated rain drops which are necessary ingredients for the fonnation of a
rainbow, as well as the legendary pot-of-gold in the front, representing everybody's
dream. Of course, the rainbow itself is a shining moment in the life of nature. We
have received many complime nts on the float design and we hope it will capture
the favorable attention of the judges. However, our approach to the float program
is to provide a float with good public appeal in the most economic al manner,
regardless of the prospects of receiving an award.
Again, the Committee gratefully acknowledges the contribution of many
individuals and organizat ions in the success of the program. In addition to the
Lodges and other organizat ions which contributed to the financial success of the
float we wish to thank members of Al Malaikah Shrine Travel Club who, for
seve;al years, have stationed their motor homes at the beginning of the Parade to
keep the riders warm and nourished prior to boarding the float, South Pasadena
Masonic Temple and Lodge whose facilities were made available and provided
lunch for riders and others after the Parade, Pasadena Temple which also made
arrangements for facilities in which to hold the New Year's Eve party for the youth
decorators, Pasadena Scottish Rite and Southern California DeMolay Center for
the use of their meeting facilities, Southern California Research Lodge for assisting
with the distribution of float flyers through their regular mailings to members ,
members of the York Rite and Shrine who provided food service to the decorator s
for more than a week, the Masonic Home at Covina for transportation of the riders
and the volunteer decorator s who turned out in hundreds to add their touch to the
beauty of the float.
Our special thanks are also extended to Grand Master Alexander, Grand
Lodge officers and the members of the California Masonic Family Forum for their
support and encouragement in this very important program of public relations. We
also appreciate the periodic assistance of the Grand Lodge office staff.

The cost of the 1996 float was approximately $83,000. Of this amount
$66,500 was th~ ~ontracted price of the float and the remainde r of the expense~
were for pubhc1ty, fund raising, food for the nearly 1,000 decorators,
c~rrespondence, postage, telephone, photography and videography and other
m1s~ellaneous expense~. The Committe e receives no Grand Lodge appropriation
for tts work an~ Committee members absorb most of their out-of-po cket expenses
to attend meetmgs and perform their various tasks.
Fund raising for this program has been very difficult and the contributions
have been less each year. Less than 25 percent of the Lodges in California and the
Grand Lodges of North A~erica have contributed sufficiently to meet the expenses
of the float. The Comm tttee felt that a more equitable plan would involve all
~odges and all m~mbers. At the 1995 Annual Communication, the Committe e
mtroduced Resolution 95- _18 request~g approval of an assessment of$1 per person
for the 1996-1997 per capita year. This Resolution failed by only I 5 votes and cast
a dark cloud on our professed support of the youth.

Recognizin~ the fund raising problems, Grand Master Charles H.

Trial Record No. 2381
In Trial Record No. 2381 , a member of Whittier Lodge No. 323 and at the
time oft.he offense, a California State Senator, was found guilty in Federal Court
of conspiracy to commit extortion under color of official rights center, extortion
color of official right and money laundering. The accused brother's conviction has
been affirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court and no further appeal of the criminal
conviction is possible.
Masonic charges were filed, a Trial Master was appointed, and the
accused was served with the charges, however, the accused Brother did not respond
to the charges. The Trial Master attempted to contact the accused brother in
Federal Prison, but the accused brother refused to see him. The Trial Master then
completed his investigation and made a finding that the charges were true and
found the accused brother guilty and set the penalty at suspension.

399

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In reviewing this case your committee is troubled by the penalty. We have
reviewed the criminal case and it is clear that the accused brother did knowingl y
and willfully extort money in exchange for his influence and vote in the State
Legislature.
Your committe e believes that the accused violated not only his Masonic
oath but also his oath of office as a State Senator and that these acts are not just
technical violations but a serious breach of the public's trust and his Masonic
obligations. Your committe e believes that this case requires the greatest penalty
and recomme nds that the penalty be raised to Expulsion .

contacting and using local Sojourner s in Constitution observanc es.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON
U.S. CONSTI TUTION OBSERV ANCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M of California:

We are all extremely pleased to serve on the U.S. Constitution Observance
Committee. The Grand Master's Proclamation stressed the responsibility of all
Masons and Americans to keep the spark of liberty alive by recognizi ng the spirit
that makes the Constitution a living and working documen t for all of us. He
directed each lodge to celebrate the birth of the Constitution by holding appropriate
activities within the lodge and communi ty.
Seve_ral actions were implemented by the committee to help the lodges in
.
thetr celebrations. Through the generosit y of the Department of Defense the
committee received a large number of Constitution Bicentennial Resource G~ides
which contained speeches. suggested programs, historical data, facsimiles of
Constitution documen ts, publicity materials, biographies of the delegates to the

Every lodge also received a memoran dum from the committe e outl ining
the resources available for Constitution Observance programs. The memo included
a copy of the California Freemason article on "Defende rs of the Constitution", a
similar article entitled "National Sojourner s, Inc. - Serving America", from the
August 1996 Scottish Rite Journal, two Short Talk Bulletin speeches on "The Bill
of Rights and Freemasonry" and "Freemasonry and the Constitution", and three
additional speeches on the Constitution. The memo also advised that the
committe e had procured six video tape programs on the Constituti on from the
National Park Service in Philadelphia which could be loaned to requesting lodges
by the Grand Lodge.
Principally through the hard work of Committe e Vice Chainnan Brad
White, a booth on U.S. Constitution Observan ce was set up at the Grand Lodge
Annual Communication in San Francisco. Constitution Observance materials were
displayed and available to the attendees and the aforemen tioned video tapes were
played. Members of the committe e alternated in tending the booth. As an added
feature, the U.S. Selective Service System prepared a display on their program
stressing the responsibility of young American s "to provide for the common
defense .. ." as set forth in the Preamble to the Constitution. The display described
the Selective Service registration responsibilities and the agency's local board
member program, with which many California Masons, including our Grand
Master, are serving as local board members . The display tied in nicely with the
committe e's Constitution Observan ce message.
Many of our lodges have done an outstandi ng job in conducting
Constitution Observance programs. Of particular note is the 1996 program held at
Knotts Berry Fann on Septembe r 14, 1996 by the 482"d Masonic District. The

400

entire Masonic family participated, including the El Bekal Shrine Potentate, Divan
and Band; the York Rite Grand Officers; the Personal Representative from the
Santa Ana Scottish Rite; eight Worshipful Masters of the District and the Masonic
Youth of the DeMolay, Job's Daughters and Rainbow Girls. The event was held
at the replica of Independence Hall. A Masonic play on the drafting of the
Constitution and a "Building the Flag" presentation by National Sojourners were
all part of this excellent program . Over 500 members of the public attended the
morning and afternoon commemoration programs. Many other programs were
held throughout the State as part of the Observance effort.
The committee continues to support the efforts of the Citizens Flag
Alliance in sponsoring an Amendment to the Constitution which would protect the
United States Flag from desecration.
The committee also responded to the Grand Master's request for a flag
pageant at the Grand Lodge Opening on Sunday afternoon. Members of the Air
Force Junior ROTC at Duncan Polytechnic High School in Fresno did a superb job
of presenting the "Flags Over California" pageant, which traced the history of the
ten flags that have flown over our State. The AFJROTC Precision Drill Team
entertained the attendees with their skill in rifle drill.
The committee held a luncheon meeting on Sunday to discuss plans for
the forthcoming year and to report on noteworthy lodge Observance programs.
The committee salutes the many lodges and brethren who have worked so
hard to insure that their lodges and communities keep the spirit of liberty alive
through their U.S. Constitution Observance Programs.
Respectfully submitted,

Most difficulties during the 1995-1996 Grand Lodge year were solved by
simple telephone consultation, however one "formal intervention" took place. As
is becoming more common, a Temple Association in Northern California found
itself facing severe financial difficulties. In an effort to increase its revenue. the
Temple Association requested that the Youth Groups which were among its tenants
change their meeting times and dates so that all weekend dates would be available
for rental of the building to non-masonic, commercial users. The Youth Groups,
who had utilized Saturday meeting dates for many years, were very upset and the
Youth Orders Committee was asked to assist in the negotiations between the Youth
Orders and the Temple Association. A member of this Committee attended a
meeting and assisted the parties to work out a compromise solution which permits
the Youth Orders to use the Temple building on some weekends, yet frees the
facility for commercial rental on some weekends. As usual, Masonic principals
prevailed once the parties sat down together to work out their respective needs.
The Youth Orders Committee again this year assisted the California
Masonic Foundation in its preparation of the Scholarship Manual, by researching
and verifying the data contained therein. The updated manual should be available
for distribution very soon.
Your Committee Chairman (and all of the Members of the Youth Orders
Committee) extend their sincere thanks to our Grand Master, Most Worshipful
Brother Charles Alexander, for permitting us to. in this small but important way,
serve our Grand Lodge. A special thank you is also given to Very Worshipful John
L. Cooper, our Grand Secretary, and to his very competent staff, who have always
given every Member of this Committee any support which has been requested,
while tolerating and minimizing the effect of any procrastination on the part of this
Committee's Chairman . The most heartfelt thanks. however, go to the Members
of our three Masonic Youth Orders. It is these young men and women who always
make our service such a joy.
